articles.title: Sybiha: 76 Energy Strikes Prove Moscow Flouts Ceasefire
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has warned that Russia is systematically expandeing targeted strikes against Ukraine’s power grid while feigning interest in diplomatic initiatives, stating that 76 targeted attacks on energy infrastructure over the past week prove Moscow has honored no commitments.
Writing on X on Sunday, Oct. 18, Sybiha stressed that offering economic accommodations or easing sanctions under such conditions only equips the Kremlin with fresh revenue to underwrite ongoing military operations ahead of winter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Its message could hardly be clearer – Moscow has not abided by any obligations,” Sybiha stated, noting that tens of thousands of Ukrainian families remain without electricity as international partners attempt to explore avenues to conclude the war.
The foreign minister reiterated figures disclosed earlier in the day by President Volodymyr Zelensky, pointing out that Russian forces carried out 76 targeted attacks against Ukrainian energy facilities since US President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” one week ago.
Sybiha added that over the preceding seven days alone, Russian forces deployed nearly 2,700 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs (KABs), and 66 missiles across Ukrainian territory, with the vast majority of missile systems consisting of high-speed ballistic weapons directed at municipal utilities.
US Tech Curbs on Kyiv Expose Allied Dependency
Simulated diplomacy and economic pressure
Ukraine’s top diplomat observed that the Kremlin is pursuing an asymmetric strategy engineered to secure international sanctions relief without altering its operational conduct or military objectives on the ground.
According to Sybiha, Moscow seeks “sanctions relief without changing its behavior, preservation of profits without accountability, and the imitation of diplomatic efforts without any commitment to stop killing Ukrainians.”
Addressing international allies and policymakers in Washington, Sybiha cautioned that lowering the economic costs of Russian aggression while civilian infrastructure faces daily bombardment directly undermines prospective peace efforts.
“Easing economic pressure under these circumstances risks giving the Kremlin additional resources to finance its war,” Sybiha emphasized.
“It is time for our partners to draw the necessary conclusions. Any serious effort to end this war must increase pressure on Moscow, restrict the revenues financing its aggression, and strengthen Ukraine’s ability to defend its cities and energy infrastructure.”
The foreign minister underlined that Russia bears unilateral responsibility for prolonging the conflict, dismissing the notion that commercial accommodations can incentivize de-escalation.
“Reducing the cost of its aggression while it continues attacking Ukraine will not bring peace,” Sybiha concluded. “It can only make further aggression easier to finance.”
Sanctions waivers and energy armistice disputes
Sybiha’s public remarks arrive amid sharp transatlantic disagreements over the Trump administration’s recent foreign policy maneuvers toward Moscow.
On Friday, Oct. 16, Trump signed an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to waive mandatory statutory penalties, including 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties targeting global purchasers of Russian hydrocarbons, just 48 hours before their scheduled implementation.
The waiver follows an Oct. 9 bilateral commercial arrangement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, under which Moscow agreed to deliver refined diesel onto international markets through 2027 to curb fuel benchmark inflation.
The shipments were authorized under a general license issued by the US Treasury Department.
While White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers argued that enforcing statutory sanctions now would impede ongoing diplomatic efforts to broker a peace settlement, Ukrainian officials have strongly contested that assessment.
Both Zelensky and Sybiha have warned that granting Moscow access to international energy markets injects direct hard currency into the Russian state budget during active military operations, validating the Kremlin’s calculation that its war effort is yielding economic dividends rather than consequences.

articles.title: Russian ‘Matryoshka’ Bot Farm Targets US Midterms With AI
articles.body:
Russian state-backed disinformation operators are deploying automated bot networks to artificially inflate view counts for fabricated videos targeting Democratic candidates and Hollywood celebrities ahead of the US midterm elections, Bloomberg News reported.
The digital influence campaign – identified by social media researchers as “Matryoshka” or “Operation Overload” – relies on artificial intelligence to generate counterfeit news broadcasts and deepfakes designed to erode public trust in electoral integrity and undermine political support for Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A review by Bloomberg of 130 fabricated videos and doctored newspaper front pages circulated between Sept. 10 and Oct. 9 revealed a systematic campaign focused almost exclusively on Democratic contenders across the country.
The findings were documented by the anonymous research group Antibot4Navalny and corroborated by US-based open-source intelligence firms Graphika and dTeam.
AI-generated celebrity fakes
The operation began circulating AI-manipulated video clips across social media platform X in early September. The media files featured synthetic likenesses of high-profile actors and musicians – including Robert De Niro, Julia Roberts, and Cher – falsely depicted as attacking Democratic politicians or encouraging viewers to join an online campaign labeled “#AllDemocratsAreCriminals.”
Additional fabricated materials mimicked established American broadcast networks to distribute unsubstantiated allegations against prominent candidates.
Trump Envoys Push Russian Gas Transit in Ukraine Peace Talks
One video carrying a counterfeit ABC News digital banner claimed that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee contesting a US Senate seat in Texas, made payments to OnlyFans models.
A spokesperson for Talarico firmly denied the assertion. Another video mimicking CBS News alleged that the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) uncovered eight undeclared real estate properties owned by Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. No public records or official disclosures substantiate the claim.
Researchers observed that Matryoshka-linked posts frequently accumulated hundreds of thousands of impressions on X within their first hour of publication. However, digital forensic data shared by Antibot4Navalny demonstrated that view counts were systematically manipulated by automated bot networks to project artificial virality.
“The number of views for Matryoshka posts can jump as high as 200,000 within the first hour but then quickly plateau,” researchers observed, noting that organic engagement follows a steady growth curve rather than a sudden spike followed by an abrupt flatline.
Forensic analysis established that the amplifying accounts had been dormant for years, possessed few followers, and generated virtually no genuine reposts or likes relative to recorded views.
Strategic shift to down-ballot races and midterms
The operational footprint of the campaign reflects a tactical evolution from previous Russian influence efforts. While past operations focused predominantly on high-stakes presidential contests, Matryoshka has broadened its parameters to target down-ballot congressional and gubernatorial races.
According to Bloomberg’s analysis, the network disseminated targeted disinformation against Democratic candidates in 20 of the 35 US Senate races and 29 of the 36 gubernatorial contests scheduled for the Nov. 3 ballot.
US intelligence agencies have warned Congress of the escalating deployment of synthetic media by foreign adversaries.
A recent assessment by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) identified Russia as the primary foreign actor deploying artificial intelligence to degrade public confidence in American democratic institutions ahead of the midterm vote.
Antibot4Navalny, which has monitored Kremlin-aligned digital networks since 2018, initially identified the Matryoshka apparatus in September 2023 as it attempted to undermine Western military assistance for Ukraine.
The operation was named after traditional Russian nesting dolls due to its operational pattern: accounts distributing one fabricated narrative frequently pivot to distributing fresh fabrications on successive days.
French government monitoring agency Viginum confirmed in early 2024 that initial seeds of Matryoshka content were routed through Russian-language channels on Telegram before migrating to Western social networks.
“It’s evolving with the technology and is more sophisticated as a result,” said Darren Linvill, professor at Clemson University and co-director of its Media Forensics Hub. “They’re actively trying to fish for more engagement.”
Disinformation backbones and physical infrastructure hits
The exposure of the Matryoshka campaign coincides with growing scrutiny of the physical and digital infrastructure that underwrites Russian computational influence operations.
Between Oct. 8 and Oct. 11, Ukrainian precision drone strikes disabled three major data centers owned by Russian technology giant Yandex in the Vladimir, Kaluga, and Ryazan regions.
The kinetic disruptions caused widespread server outages across Russian enterprise networks and triggered a sharp reduction in automated web requests originating from Russian server clusters.
According to network intelligence provider Cloudflare Radar, automated bot traffic from Yandex’s sovereign network plunged immediately following the facility strikes.
The computational downtime was followed by reports from digital monitors across Europe describing a marked decline in automated polarization.
Polish open-source defense analyst Jarosław Wolski observed a noticeable contraction in coordinated online attacks pitting Polish citizens against Ukrainian refugees, alongside a temporary drop in bot-driven engagement boosting fringe political parties in Germany.
President Volodymyr Zelensky referenced the operational ripple effects on Oct. 12, noting that precision interdiction against Russian digital nodes resulted in “less hatred, less discord, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots.”
Western security agencies maintain that Moscow’s influence operations increasingly blur the boundary between cognitive warfare and algorithmic manipulation.
Previous legal actions by the US Department of Justice disrupted 968 AI-powered bot profiles operated under the direction of state broadcaster RT and the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB), alongside the “Doppelganger” network of cloned media domains, underscoring allied efforts to dismantle coordinated influence operations ahead of the November vote.

articles.title: Netanyahu warns Israel could lose US support, seeks 450 billion shekels in extra defense spending
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Sunday that Israel could face a hostile U.S. administration in the future, potentially threatening its military assistance and strategic relationship with Washington, and said the country must develop new international alliances. At the same time, he announced plans to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels in additional defense spending over the next decade.
Netanyahu made the remarks during an event at which he presented his security doctrine, nine days before Israel's October 27 election. Just hours later, U.S. President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu's reelection bid for the first time during the current campaign.
"In two years, a president, man or woman, could come to power who is very hostile to Israel," Netanyahu said. "How would you deal with that? How would you operate in relation to the United States? And beyond that, what solutions would be necessary?"
His remarks came against the possibility that a future U.S. administration could suspend military assistance to Israel or even join international sanctions and an arms embargo against the country.
Netanyahu said Israel must use the remaining years of Trump's presidency to strengthen its position while preparing for a potentially dramatic shift in American policy.
"First, we must do everything we can during these two years, and during the following two years, in the American arena, through good times and bad," he said. "The second thing is to create other alliances. That is what I am working on now with many countries in our region and outside it. India is not a small country, and there are many others."
He pointed to political developments in Latin America as another opportunity to expand Israel's network of allies.
"There is a major shift in Latin America, and there could be an enormous change in Brazil in just a few days," Netanyahu said. "We must expand our pool of alliances and develop capabilities that make us valuable to everyone."
He also addressed Israel's strained relations with European countries, accusing some governments of publicly condemning Israel while continuing to seek cooperation with it.
"Countries that condemn us, and they have some nerve, by the way, condemn us and then come to us," he said. "I tell them: It depends on you. It depends on how you behave."
Netanyahu argued that Israel still possesses diplomatic leverage but would need considerable international expertise to navigate changes in Washington and other capitals.
In a separate social media post Sunday, Netanyahu appeared to acknowledge the possibility of a change in U.S. leadership, describing Trump's remaining time in office as an opportunity to advance Israel's strategic objectives.
"We have another two years of my friend President Trump's term, and this is exactly the time to complete our major missions on every front," he wrote.
On defense spending, Netanyahu said he intended to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels over the coming decade to strengthen Israel's military capabilities. An additional defense spending package of approximately 350 billion shekels had previously been agreed upon, according to earlier reports.
Addressing the future size of the Israel Defense Forces, Netanyahu said the military would have to expand, although technological advances, particularly artificial intelligence, could reduce some of its manpower requirements.
"As for a large army or a small army, the IDF definitely needs to grow," he said. "It will grow, but not at the rate we might have expected because AI reduces many requirements. Still, it needs to grow, and for that, of course, you need to allocate both funding and personnel."
He added: "I am putting about 450 billion shekels into this so that we have the capabilities and the teeth."
Turning to Iran, Netanyahu said the regime remained a threat despite what he described as severe military and economic damage inflicted on it. He warned that Tehran would seek to rebuild its nuclear program, develop other unconventional weapons and restore its regional network of allied armed groups.
"Like cancer, this will not end as long as that regime remains in place," he said. "It will try to recover, renew its nuclear program, renew other unconventional weapons programs and rebuild the axis."
Netanyahu claimed that Israel had already accomplished approximately 90% of its objectives against Iran and described the Iranian leadership as severely weakened.
"Why aren't people taking to the streets? Because right now they are being killed. Simply killed. They are killing or wounding tens of thousands of their own people. That is the nature of this regime," he said.
He then explicitly stated that his policy was aimed at bringing down the Iranian government. "Our plan is very comprehensive and very determined, to bring about the downfall of the regime," Netanyahu said. "That is my plan. That is the directive I have given all the security agencies, and that is what will happen."
Netanyahu also discussed Israel's relationship with Russia, describing it as one based on competing national interests rather than consistent cooperation.
"We speak when necessary," he said. "But Russia has its interests, and we have the interests of the State of Israel, and they do not always overlap. Sometimes they even clash."
He cited Russia's cooperation with Iran during the war in Ukraine as an example of conflicting interests and also raised the issue of anti-Israel bot networks spreading what he described as extreme antisemitic content.
"We raise all these issues, and we do so very clearly," Netanyahu said. "And when there is an opportunity to cooperate, we do that as well."
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the opposition Yashar! party and a former IDF chief of staff, sharply criticized Netanyahu's presentation, describing it as an empty political exercise rather than a serious national security strategy.
"Nine days before the election and three years after the gravest failure and disaster in Israel's history, with every war front still open, Netanyahu decided to present his 'security doctrine' to the public," Eisenkot said.
"Two hollow pages, full of slogans that have nothing whatsoever to do with a security doctrine, reveal more than anything the strategic vacuum Netanyahu has left the State of Israel in and his disregard for the security of Israeli citizens."
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of attempting to manipulate public opinion and spread fear ahead of the election.
"This is Netanyahu's method: manipulating perceptions, frightening people and trying to divert attention from the parade of lies and racism surrounding his campaign tonight," he said.

articles.title: Kremlin says Ukrainian attacks won’t change war aims as Kyiv hits Saint Petersburg
articles.body:
Kremlin says Ukrainian attacks won’t change war aims as Kyiv hits Saint Petersburg
- The Kremlin said Ukrainian attacks on Russian cities will not change its war aims, after Kyiv hit Saint Petersburg with its biggest drone strike since 2022 and set an oil refinery ablaze.
- Russia said the attack killed one person, injured others, damaged homes and infrastructure, and forced airport limits, while officials claimed 144 drones were shot down.
- Zelensky said Russia broke the “energy ceasefire” 76 times and warned of a winter “blackout”, as peace talks stall and both sides keep trading strikes.
AI generated
SAINT PETERSBURG – The Kremlin on Oct 18 said Ukrainian large-scale attacks on Russian cities will not change its war aims as Kyiv hit Saint Petersburg with the biggest drone attack on Vladimir Putin’s hometown since 2022, setting an oil refinery ablaze.
Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg’s historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot in night time strikes that killed one person.
The attack came as Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of violating an “energy ceasefire” announced by US leader Donald Trump 76 times as he warned Russia planned a “blackout” in Ukraine before winter.
Kyiv struck Saint Petersburg as its ties with Washington strained massively in recent days, with Trump waiving sanctions on Russia and striking a deal with Moscow on diesel.
Ukraine and its European allies have worried the White House is siding with Moscow, which launched Europe’s worst war since WWII in 2022.
Saint Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
The authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Flights were restricted at the city’s Pulkovo airport, Beglov said, adding that 12 housing blocks were also damaged.
Russia’s VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit in the city and Ozon – Russia’s second largest retailer – also reported a hit on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the 2022 war.
Ukraine has attacked Moscow and Saint Petersburg throughout the Kremlin’s dragging offensive but large-scale hits on Russia’s main cities are rare.
“The Kyiv regime is putting up a fight, but that cannot change the course of events,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media.
Russia’s offensive against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.
Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
US-led peace talks have not led to a breakthrough.
In a fifth year of war, few see a way out.
Putin appeared in military uniform this week and repeated Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
‘Dreadful routine of war’
“There’s a general feeling: they’re attacking, we’re attacking – it’s become the dreadful routine of war,” 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Sergei, another resident of the city who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
“I don’t know if I was scared, what must be will be,” he told AFP.
“My main thought was that petrol would run out at the petrol stations and I’d better fill up.”
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier in 2026.
Leningrad governor Drozdenko said 20,000 people were without power in the town of Yanino, where a substation was hit.
He said a woman and three children were hospitalised “with symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning” in the region after drone debris fell on a house, causing a fire.
“I woke up at night, heard bangs, looked out of the window and there was a fire,” 40-year-old Saint Petersburg resident Igor told AFP.
“They’re getting on my nerves already,” he added, referring to Ukraine.
‘Bet on war is paying off’
In Ukraine, Zelensky said Russian strikes hit substations in four Ukrainian regions, leaving “tens of thousands of families without power.”
The Ukrainian authorities said Russian attacks killed at least three people on Oct 18, including a 27-year-old woman in Zaporizhzhia and two people in the western Volyn region bordering Poland.
The Saint Petersburg attack came a day after Zelensky called on allies to keep up pressure on Moscow as he denounced Trump’s move to block new sanctions on Russia.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” Zelensky said on Oct 18, adding: “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”
Trump this week blocked a package of new sanctions on Russia which was meant to target Putin, as well as Russia’s energy and defence sectors.
He also signed an agreement with Moscow in October to buy diesel, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of elections.
“It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance,” Zelensky said on Oct 18. AFP

articles.title: IRGC profiting from sex trafficking of Iranian women, using children for proxy wars - JCFA
articles.body:
Iranian women trafficked for sex, undocumented migrants, children, and refugees are being exploited by the Islamic Republic, and specifically the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), to finance and support its proxy wars across the region, according to a new analysis published last week by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs.
Ella Rosenberg, a senior research fellow at the JCFA and a member of the Dvorah Forum, said Iran’s legal framework allows the regime to project an image of compliance with international anti-trafficking regulations while relying on flawed legislation that falls short of international standards and fails to adequately protect victims.
She noted specifically that the Islamic Republic conflates human trafficking with migrant smuggling, and the regime has consistently refused to ratify the 2000 United Nations Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons (the Palermo Protocol).
IRGC directly benefiting from sex trafficking, Israeli study finds
Beyond failing to protect victims, Rosenberg assessed that the IRGC directly benefits from human trafficking. She noted that the IRGC uses the sex trafficking sector, often facilitated by the regime through temporary marriages, as a major source of income.
Rosenberg described Iran as a source, transit, and destination country for the sex trafficking of women and girls, citing widespread poverty, systemic corruption, and economic mismanagement as contributing factors.
She argued that Article 1041 of Iran’s Civil Code, which permits girls to marry at 13 and younger girls to marry with parental permission and court approval, has helped normalize the sexual exploitation of minors. Rosenberg also linked the practice of nikah mut’ah, a temporary marriage contract agreed upon for a predetermined period, to the exploitation of women and girls and their vulnerability to organized trafficking networks.
Trafficking networks move victims within Iran and across its borders into neighboring countries, including Iraq, with the alleged support of the IRGC, according to Rosenberg. She argued that the scale of cross-border sex trafficking could not be sustained without the corps’ complicity, given its role in border control and the intelligence apparatus’s oversight of internal security checkpoints and airports.
Adding more weight to her analysis, Human rights groups, including IHR Monitor and HRANA, have documented allegations that IRGC commanders accepted bribes to facilitate the passage of trafficking victims. Rosenberg added that the IRGC profits directly from the exploitation of Iranian women by taxing the commercial sex trade.
IRGC exploiting Afghan, Pakistani refugees
In addition to financially benefiting from human trafficking, the JCFA report claimed that the IRGC’s Quds Force and the Basij systematically traffic undocumented migrants, refugees, and children to “sustain their proxy wars across the Middle East.”
The IRGC exploits vulnerable populations, particularly Afghan and Pakistani refugees, to recruit fighters through deception, financial coercion, and threats of deportation, she argued. Individuals harvested from these communities are coerced into joining proxy militias like the Fatemiyoun and the Zainabiyoun brigades, for deployment in foreign countries like Iraq.
Additionally, in violation of international law, the Basij systematically recruits and coerces Iranian children as young as 12 into military indoctrination and combat support roles. This was argued to be a severe form of human trafficking, as the recruitment exploits children’s vulnerability to coerce them into hazardous, involuntary servitude in military environments. Though JCFA warns of the abuse of children aged 12 and up, The Jerusalem Post has previously reported on the death of an 11-year-old Basij member who was killed at a checkpoint in Iran.
Rather than directly profiting from the trafficking of vulnerable individuals into the IRGC, Rosenberg put that the financial gain can be categorized as cost avoidance rather than revenue. She argued that rather than deploying trained members of the IRGC, which the regime would have to pay and has invested in, the revolutionary guards can deploy underpaid or unpaid vulnerable groups who are deemed disposable because of their lack of funded training.
Such deployments were estimated to save the Islamic Republic billions of dollars in military expenditure, freeing funds to be redirected into the IRGC’s domestic corporate monopolies and regional terror financing networks.
Again, Iran’s “tax” system also allows it to benefit from migrants transiting from Pakistan and Afghanistan hoping to reach Europe through Iran and Turkey.
The migrants are also routinely subjected to debt bondage, extortion, and forced labor in Iran’s informal agricultural and construction sectors to pay off exorbitant smuggling fees by criminal networks who pay protection money to the IRGC. This alone is estimated to generate billions of dollars for Iran’s shadow economy. creates a multi-billion-dollar shadow economy.
Focus on Iran's nuclear program may distract from IRGC human trafficking
Rosenberg shared that Iran was able to continue to exploit these systems as sanctions from the EU and US have primarily focused on Tehran’s nuclear proliferation, ballistic missile development, support for regional terrorism, and suppression of domestic dissent. Failing to also sanction the IRGC and the front companies it uses for human trafficking continues to provide Tehran a lifeline.
Given that the funds raised by human trafficking are often liquid, Rosenberg also alerted to the fact that it was hard for international systems to monitor how much wealth Iran is accumulating through these streams. Individuals involved in facilitating or covering for the regime-backed smuggling networks are therefore allowed to continue to travel, utilize regional banks, and manage front companies without fear of asset freezes or international arrest warrants.
To prevent Iran from continuing to profit from human trafficking, Rosenberg advised that the US Treasury Department should utilize the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act specifically to designate IRGC border commanders, Basij recruitment officers, and complicit Iranian law enforcement officials for their roles in labor and sex trafficking.
She added that the European Commission must also leverage the Sixth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (AMLD6) to require European financial institutions to monitor illicit financial flows generated by Iranian trafficking networks aggressively.

articles.title: Built as a cheap Shahed lookalike, Russia’s Gerbera now flies with a 10-kg warhead and an incendiary bag
articles.body:
Russia has started fitting its enlarged Gerbera-2 drones with a 10-kg warhead and an extra bag of incendiary mixture, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported on 18 October. The setup is designed to start a fire where the drone hits and is probably meant for attacks on critical infrastructure and warehouses, the outlet said.
Russia’s industry makes about 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, Ukraine’s military intelligence has said, and Russian strikes have destroyed 2.1 million m² of Ukraine’s modern warehouse space since the full-scale invasion began. A cheap drone that carries fire adds one more threat for air defenses that already let nearly half of Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds through.
A fire bag behind the warhead
Ukrainian Telegram channel Polkovnyk HSh posted photos of the payload on 17 October. Gerbera-2 strike and reconnaissance drones had begun to appear with a 10-kg high-explosive fragmentation-incendiary warhead and an extra package of incendiary mixture, the channel wrote. They navigate with Kometa-M12, a 12-element antenna array designed to resist jamming, it added.
Russian drones set their own detonators at altitude: Why cutting wires won’t save from new Gerberas?
In the photos, the incendiary mixture sits in a separate soft plastic tank behind the main warhead, Militarnyi said. Gerbera-2s have been seen with warheads of 4 to 10 kg depending on range, while strike versions of the original Gerbera usually carried up to 5 kg, the outlet noted.
Half a Shahed engine
Russia has mainly fielded the Gerbera, a cheap drone shaped like a Shahed, as a decoy and reconnaissance platform flying alongside Shahed-type strike drones. It has also used bigger Gerberas to drop FPV drones.
Serhii Beskrestnov, now an adviser to Ukraine’s president, flagged a much bigger Gerbera in Ukraine’s skies on 7 August. The Gerbera-2 has a larger airframe, a reshaped wing, and a bigger tail fin, Militarnyi said. In August, the outlet reported it had a stronger piston engine: half of the one in the Shahed-type Geran-2, at about 275 cm³. Production of these engines was set up at the Izhevsk Motorcycle Plant, according to preliminary information the outlet cited.
Russia equips Geran attack drones with image-based navigation using Google map imagery, reducing reliance on satellite navigation that Ukraine can jam, defense adviser warns
Earlier versions ran on a Chinese DLE60 model-aircraft engine of about 61 cm³. The switch was likely possible because Geran-2 engine output partly freed up as jet-powered Geran-4s took a growing share of Russia’s drones, Militarnyi said. The Gerbera-2’s fuel tank also holds up to 63 liters, against 10 liters on the original.
One reached Poland’s Baltic coast
In September, a drone preliminarily identified as a Gerbera-2 was recovered from the Baltic Sea near Rusinowo, on Poland’s coast. It carried a high-explosive fragmentation warhead of about 4 kg, a Polish military prosecutor said.

articles.title: Intensifying drone attacks on ships in Black Sea bring war ever closer to Nato shores
articles.body:
The first the crew of the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria knew of an attack on a cargo ship in their country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea in the early hours of 6 October was a distant explosion 70 miles off the coastal town of Byala.
The Turkish-owned Alfa Watan, heading for the Romanian port of Sulina, had been struck by suspected Russian air and naval drones. Arriving on the scene, Dioscuria found an overturned lifeboat and lifejackets in the water. There was no sign, however, of Alfa Watan’s crew of 10.
Six days later drones struck another ship off the coast of Bulgaria, HS Dignity. Eleven crew members died.
By Thursday, the attacks had encroached on Romania’s airspace and territorial water. Two chemical tankers, Wine Trader and Yara J, were attacked and left burning. Seven more sailors were missing.
The attacks on six ships in 10 days – the Able and Chelsea-3 were also hit – marked a dramatic escalation in a maritime conflict that is pressing on Nato’s borders.
While global attention has focused on the risks for sailors travelling through the strait of Hormuz, in recent months it is the Black Sea that has emerged as the more dangerous passage, with more sailors lost in a week and a half than US service members killed in the entire Iran war.
The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has warned that there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.
Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey, has noted a sharp increase in the tempo of attacks beginning in July. Russian forces are estimated to be responsible for 80% of them.
The recent loss of life, he suggests, has been exacerbated by “double tap” attacks involving aerial and surface drones, the latter often carrying up to half a tonne of explosive payloads. Smaller vessels that primarily use the Danube canal system have sunk rapidly.
“While attacks against merchant vessels in the Black Sea are not new, we are seeing an escalation both in terms of the number of attacks and in the geographical scope,” Alexa said.
The profile of vessels being attacked – that is, ships trading with Ukraine – had not changed, he added. “The Russian intent is clear, which is to degrade the export of Ukrainian grain and agricultural products.”
The result has been a precipitous fall in the number of vessels visiting Ukraine. Insurance rates have soared, and seafarers and operators have become increasingly reluctant to operate in the Black Sea basin, even on ships unconnected with Ukrainian cargoes.
The vast majority of the more than 60 fatalities of seafarers in the Black Sea since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 have occurred in the past year. In September the Joint War Committee, representing the London insurance market, moved to extend the high-risk areas of the Black Sea to include the whole of the basin, excluding the territorial waters of Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria and Georgia.
The threat is not confined to the Black Sea itself. Attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have also increased sharply in the past year.
A number of factors are driving the expansion and escalation of the conflict towards the shores of Nato countries, say experts. Russia has responded to a geographical expansion of Ukrainian strikes on its shadow fleet of oil tankers by intensifying strikes on Ukrainian agricultural cargoes – a key component of Kyiv’s economy.
As ships sought safer passage further from the coastlines, so the threat has changed: from naval mines to drones, with ever longer ranges.
Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said after the sinking of the Alfa Watan: “Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea.”
In a statement at the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, Col Joby Rimmer, a senior British military adviser, said: “Attacks that fail to distinguish between military objectives and civilian vessels, or that are expected to cause excessive incidental harm to civilians and civilian vessels in relation to the anticipated military advantage, may violate international humanitarian law and the UN convention on the law of the sea.
“Each attack raises the risk to crews of every nationality, drives up insurance costs and restricts the flow of food to those who depend on it. The UK is deeply concerned by the far-reaching consequences of successive crises across the global maritime domain. Stable and secure sea lanes are a global common good from which we all benefit.”
Operators have warned of the wider impact on trade in the Black Sea, including from Bulgarian ports. In a recent interview on Bulgarian television, the shipping agency owner Todor Georgiev warned the Black Sea was in danger of becoming a “dead zone”.
“Whenever the Russians are caught having struck a ship with one of their drones, they claim the vessel was carrying weapons,” he said. “Weapons are not being transported to Ukraine via the Black Sea.”
Rumen Radev, Bulgaria’s prime minister, has described the attacks in the vicinity of his country’s territorial waters as “absolutely unacceptable”.
Bulgarian officials are calling for the EU and Nato to support the efforts to enhance security, while working with Turkey and Romania on increased regional security.
Although they have refused to attribute blame to Russia, officials have said there is “no logic” for Ukraine to attack its own shipments.
“We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side,” said Radev. “However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation.”
As Russian strikes on shipping move ever closer to the borders of Nato members, they pose mounting security challenges to the mutual defence organisation, which is already confronting Moscow’s growing hybrid warfare across Europe. There is speculation that the affected Nato countries may be forced to invoke article 4 of the organisation’s treaty, a step below the article 5 invocation of mutual self defence.
Triggered twice already around the Ukraine war – in the immediate aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and by Poland in 2025 after Russian drones violated Warsaw’s airspace – it calls for formal crisis discussions on a security threat.
On Thursday Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, met Radev and Nicușor Dan, Romania’s president, to discuss security in the Black Sea. Rutte said: “Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
Another consequence of the escalating attacks is the renewed danger of a global food crisis. Ukraine and Russia are major exporters of grain, as is Romania.
“We’re looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery,” said Oana Toiu, the Romanian foreign minister, at a security conference in Warsaw last week. “It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence.”
Damien Chevallier, the director of maritime safety at the UN’s International Maritime Organization, warned last month of the long-term impact on shipping caused by attacks linked to the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
“With rising casualties across the Black Sea, Red Sea and strait of Hormuz, being a seafarer has become a genuinely dangerous profession,” he said. “Seafarers are not trained to deal with threats from actions which are linked to wider security issues or geopolitical situations.
“What makes this moment genuinely unprecedented is not just the number of incidents, but the pattern behind them. Shipping has become a deliberate instrument of geopolitical leverage.”

articles.title: Latvia’s combat-tested ground drone shows off in Finland
articles.body:
- Latvian company NATRIX demonstrated its combat-tested unmanned ground vehicle at Millog’s UGV Demo 2026 in Mikkeli, Finland, on Oct. 8.
- The vehicle showed forest mobility, obstacle crossing, cargo transport and remote control before Finnish military, border guard and police officials.
Latvian company NATRIX, already a supplier of ground drones to Latvia’s armed forces, showed its battle-tested unmanned ground vehicle to Finnish military and security officials on Oct. 8, driving it through forest terrain and hauling cargo at an unmanned ground systems demonstration in Mikkeli, Finland.
The event was organized by Millog, the Finnish defense maintenance company that services much of the Finnish Defence Forces’ equipment, and brought together several manufacturers of ground drones. NATRIX attended with its Finnish partner Armatech Finland, the company said in a LinkedIn post, and showed the vehicle to representatives from several branches of the Finnish Defence Forces, the Finnish Ministry of Defence, the Finnish Border Guard, the Police of Finland and international military delegations.
In its live demonstration, NATRIX said the vehicle showed its mobility and ability to cross obstacles in rough forest terrain, carried cargo, and was driven remotely by an operator. The company also briefed visitors on lessons from the platform’s use in combat.
The NATRIX UGV is a compact, battery-powered vehicle built for front-line resupply, casualty evacuation and reconnaissance support. The company says it can carry more than 200 kg (440 pounds) of cargo and can be fitted with a NATO-standard stretcher to bring out wounded troops, and that its communications use several backup channels to stay connected in jammed environments.
The platform began combat testing in Ukraine’s Donbas region in early 2025, after the first vehicles were funded through a donation campaign run by Latvian public media and the Ziedot.lv charity platform. Co-founder Gatis Vectirāns said at the time that a fully charged vehicle could travel about 20 km (12 miles), and that Ukrainian operators had praised its power and build quality, Latvian public broadcaster LSM reported.
In April 2026, Latvia’s Ministry of Defence signed contracts with NATRIX and two other Latvian companies, Brasa Defence Systems and LV-Teh, to supply domestically made ground drones and gradually introduce them into regular units of the National Armed Forces, The Defence Blog reported. The deals followed live demonstrations on military training ranges in 2025 and include support, repair and modernization, as well as the right for Latvia to order more systems quickly under the same framework.
Ukraine now relies heavily on ground drones to move ammunition, food and water to positions where Russian surveillance drones make vehicle and foot traffic dangerous, and to evacuate wounded soldiers under fire. Finland, which shares a 1,340 km (830-mile) border with Russia, has been studying those lessons as it expands its own forces.
NATRIX is developing autonomous features such as “follow me” and automatic return modes and plans to add mine-clearing equipment and weapon integration. Last month the company also unveiled a separate ground drone designed to patrol critical infrastructure such as energy sites, ports and airports, and it said the Mikkeli demonstration opened talks with Finnish defense and security officials on possible future cooperation.

articles.title: Rubio: Ukraine Does Not Have Access to Starshield
articles.body:
Ukraine currently lacks access to the specialized military-grade Starshield satellite network and has requested the technology to conduct deep-interdiction strikes inside Russia, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
Speaking to journalists in comments released by the US Department of State, Rubio clarified the distinction between SpaceX’s standard commercial Starlink communications framework and the dedicated Starshield architecture operated under contract with the US Department of Defense.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defense product, a military product,” Rubio stated.
“That is something that the United States military uses. It’s not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that’s under conversation. It’s under discussion right now how they would want to use it.”
Responding to questions regarding reports of technological throttling, Rubio directly refuted claims that the Trump administration had mandated bandwidth or velocity caps on terminals operating in Ukrainian combat sectors.
“I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield. They do not have Starshield now. They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” Rubio emphasized.
“Those are two different products.”
Zelensky Calls Trump’s Sanctions Waiver a Mistake
White House denies intentional velocity caps
Rubio pushed back against assertions by President Volodymyr Zelensky that artificial operational constraints imposed on Starlink terminals inside Ukraine were deliberate administrative measures.
“I don’t know what Zelensky said. I’m not sure Zelensky knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.
“Nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored. It’s back to where it was before. That’s Starlink, though. They were using Starlink for their drones.”
Addressing media reports suggesting executive coordination to limit unmanned systems, the secretary of state characterized the allegations as completely unfounded.
“Nothing to do with the White House. I saw a report on that the other day. It’s just categorically false,” Rubio told reporters.
“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it. But my understanding is it’s back up and running. That’s what I read – that’s what we heard two days ago.”
Zelensky’s 161 km/h disclosure
Rubio’s comments follow detailed disclosures delivered on Saturday, Oct. 17, by President Zelensky, who revealed that Starlink terminals operating inside Ukrainian territory had been subjected to a strict velocity limitation of 161 km/h (100 mph).
According to Zelensky, whenever equipped domestic platforms exceeded the 161 km/h threshold, satellite connections automatically severed, causing operators to lose control of unmanned interceptors in mid-flight.
The velocity cap effectively disabled domestic drone interceptors tasked with neutralizing high-speed, turbojet-powered Russian Shahed loitering munitions, which penetrate sovereign airspace at speeds exceeding 400 km/h (250 mph).
Zelensky highlighted that Ukrainian technical teams conducted cross-border comparative evaluations, sending Starlink-equipped vehicles into EU territory, where the devices operated uninterrupted at velocities of 180 km/h (112 mph). The Ukrainian leader argued that the trials confirmed the restrictions were geographically targeted at Ukrainian airspace rather than stemming from global software glitches.
The Starshield controversy
The technological dispute underscores widening geopolitical friction between Washington and Kyiv over long-range interdiction limits and commercial communications dependencies.
Rubio’s denials echo statements by US President Donald Trump, who told that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered operational caps on Ukraine’s military communications, asserting that “everything is the same as it’s always been.”
However, both official denials contradict reporting by The Telegraph, which cited four sources familiar with the matter stating that Musk directly proposed satellite service limitations to Trump, who approved the measure, clearing the way for the Pentagon to restrict Starshield functionality.
Sources cited in the report claimed Musk sought to shift public accountability onto the White House amid concerns over potential consumer boycotts across European markets following civilian casualties in Kyiv.

articles.title: U.S. Army tests Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessels as drone carriers
articles.body:
- Ukrainian-built Magura drone boats took part in the U.S. Army’s Bayonet Quest 26 exercise in Michigan, launching aerial drones from a platform on the hull.
- The same boat family sank a target ship during Balikatan 2026 in the Philippines on April 24, 2026.
Ukraine’s Magura uncrewed surface vessels, the drone boats that have sunk Russian warships in the Black Sea, took part in a U.S. Army exercise in Michigan, where they were used as floating launch pads for aerial drones.
The boats appeared during Bayonet Quest 26, which the 7th Infantry Division, part of Multi-Domain Command-Pacific, ran across Michigan from Sept. 26 to Oct. 6, 2026. The division said soldiers used the exercise to test autonomous systems and uncrewed aircraft as it experiments with how new technology can extend sensing, reach and decision-making.
According to images and materials released by the division, the exercise included crewed-uncrewed maritime testing that paired a Mk VI patrol boat with autonomous systems, giving the U.S. Army a look at how the two could work together in complex terrain. The Magura boats, built by Ukrainian manufacturer UFORCE, carried a dedicated platform on the front of the hull from which aerial drones took off.
The 7th Infantry Division did not say how many Magura boats took part, which model was used, or what type of aerial drones they carried.
The Michigan exercise is the second publicly known use of the Magura family by U.S. forces this year. During Balikatan 2026, the largest annual U.S.-Philippines military exercise, Magura boats destroyed a decommissioned target ship in a live-fire maritime strike off Itbayat in the Batanes islands on April 24, 2026. UFORCE confirmed on June 8 that its vessels had taken part, after The Defence Blog reported that U.S. special forces had sunk a ship with Ukrainian-designed drone boats.
Magura boats became one of Ukraine’s best-known weapons after its military intelligence used them to strike Russian Black Sea Fleet ships near Crimea, forcing much of the fleet to move away from the peninsula. Ukraine has since developed versions armed with missiles and machine guns, and in 2025 Ukrainian military intelligence said Magura boats armed with air-to-air missiles had shot down Russian fighter jets over the Black Sea.
Using a drone boat to carry and launch aerial drones extends how far a small craft can see and strike without putting a crewed ship close to the target. Ukraine has used drone boats in a similar way to carry smaller strike drones toward Russian-held coastlines, and the U.S. Army has been looking at uncrewed boats for its units in the Pacific, where many operations would play out among islands and along coastlines.
The 7th Infantry Division, based at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state, was reorganized under Multi-Domain Command-Pacific as part of the U.S. Army’s efforts to prepare for operations in the Indo-Pacific region.

articles.title: Lavrov’s pivotal Monday visit to Tehran with a mediation flavor
articles.body:
Lavrov’s pivotal Monday visit to Tehran with a mediation flavor
Arman-e-Emrooz analyzed Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s upcoming visit to Tehran on Monday. Reports suggest that the trip is part of Russia’s ongoing mediation efforts between Iran and the United States. In recent months, Moscow has sought to position itself as a facilitator in reducing tensions between Tehran and Washington.
The timing of the visit coincides with US review of sanctions and measures related to the so-called shadow fleet, highlighting the complexity of the current situation. On one hand, the United States faces domestic pressure to lower energy prices ahead of elections. On the other, Iran is seeking meaningful economic relief. These circumstances have created an environment in which both sides may be inclined toward tactical flexibility. The meeting between Lavrov and Araghchi could represent an important step in that direction, provided both parties enter discussions with a shared understanding of existing realities and align their expectations with practical possibilities. The outcome of the visit could influence developments in the coming weeks.
Khorasan: Trump, the mother of all lies
Khorasan addressed Trump’s recent claim about using the “Mother of All Bombs” in a future strike against Iran. Trump is making such threats at a time when the economic consequences of tensions in the region have significantly increased costs related to energy and essential goods for American families and other countries, putting additional pressure on his administration. The paper described Trump as a gambler seeking a face-saving exit from the Iran war quagmire. After previous efforts, including military deployments to the region and severe economic pressure campaigns that were expected to quickly force Iran into submission, failed to achieve their goals, Trump has now turned to the rhetoric of the “Mother of All Bombs.” The article contends that the purpose of such statements is to create psychological pressure inside Iran and gain leverage in ongoing exchanges of messages between the two sides.
Shargh: An open-ended American policy or an open-ended Iranian one?
Shargh devoted its editorial to decision-making regarding the current conflict. The newspaper argued that decisions made today are linked not only to the future of 90 million Iranians but, in some respects, to global developments as well. The editorial proposed moving beyond the simple pro-war versus pro-peace divide and distinguishing among three separate positions: first, ending the war at any cost; second, negotiating an end to the conflict while preserving core national red lines; and third, continuing resistance until specific political and security conditions are achieved. This conceptual distinction is important for policymaking. A person who favors negotiations does not necessarily support surrender or territorial fragmentation, just as someone who considers resistance necessary is not necessarily indifferent to its human and economic costs. The paper argues that recognizing this distinction prevents an “open-ended American policy” from automatically being interpreted as an “open-ended Iranian policy,” which it describes as the key issue.
Ettelaat: Possibility of a longer conflict process
Ettelaat examined possible future scenarios for the conflict. US demands have shifted from redefining Iran’s regional role to focusing on the nuclear issue and the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Iran’s demands have reportedly evolved from direct compensation by Washington to a conditional investment fund financed by other parties. Nevertheless, the newspaper argued that two major ambiguities remain unresolved and may even have deepened as a result of the conflict. Continued American pressure is said to intensify divisions among Iranian elites and increase their reluctance to take the first step. Washington, however, may interpret this hesitation as evidence that pressure is working and therefore warrants further action. According to the analysis, diplomacy has reached a deadlock. As US midterm elections draw closer, there remains a possibility that the conflict will add another chapter to the historical memories each side holds of the other, extending a process that has already lasted for more than four decades.
Hamshahri: The impact of war and economic tensions on US elections
Hamshahri focused on concerns influencing American voters. The newspaper argued that economic conditions and the conflict involving Iran have become major public concerns. Rising prices for gasoline, diesel fuel, and essential goods, along with inflation and growing concerns about living costs, have increased pressure on the Trump administration. The paper noted that these concerns are reflected in public opinion polls and political analyses. At the same time, the Iran conflict remains among voters’ principal worries. Hamshahri also linked these concerns to allegations regarding corruption and the financial interests of individuals close to Trump in connection with the conflict. As a result, the newspaper concluded that the economic pressures associated with the conflict cannot be ignored in assessing the US political climate. According to its analysis, these pressures have fueled public dissatisfaction and could present a significant challenge for Republicans in upcoming elections.

articles.title: Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’
articles.body:
Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’
US secretary of state says Ukraine has requested access to military-grade version of Starlink for strikes deep inside Russia.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite service, is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but a request from Kyiv to access the system for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Rubio stressed Starshield’s distinction with Starlink, the internet service provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defence product, a military product,” said Rubio, in comments released by the Department of State.
“They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” he added. “That’s under conversation.”
Launched in 2022 and provided to the US government, Starshield is designed for military use as it allows for deeper encryption to process sensitive information. SpaceX says it is primarily used by US defence agencies and other “government partners”.
Last week, Ukrainian officials said restrictions on Starlink terminals had slowed some drones on the battlefield, as Ukraine tries to hold back Russian forces in their nearly five-year war.
In his comments at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, Rubio also rejected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s suggestion that the reported disruption to Starlink services in Ukraine on Wednesday was deliberate.
“Well, I don’t know what Zelenskyy said. I’m not sure Zelenskyy knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that the satellites are not tracking antennas on flying objects travelling faster than 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour). This is affecting Ukrainian drones in their defence against Russian jet-powered drones and in their own medium-range attacks, he added.
Rubio said the US had not ordered Starlink speeds to be reduced and that the service had reportedly been restored to its previous level.
“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it,” he said, calling the reports “categorically false”.
The remarks came as US President Donald Trump drew criticism from Democrats and Republicans after waiving sanctions on Russia and countries that buy its oil and gas, days before the restrictions were due to take effect under a law he signed last month.
Zelenskyy also criticised the sanctions waiver on Saturday, saying easing pressure on Russia would encourage further attacks.
“Financial rewards for [President Vladimir] Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy posted on social media, urging the US to maintain pressure on Moscow.

articles.title: Romania downs two Russian jet drones near Sulina, days before NATO allies meet on Black Sea security
articles.body:
Two Romanian F-16s shot down two jet-powered Russian Geran attack drones over Romania’s territorial waters near Sulina on the evening of 17 October, Romania’s Defense Ministry said. The ministry released cockpit images of the mission the next day, as NATO allies prepare to discuss Black Sea security at a special session Romania requested.
This comes as Moscow continues its air attacks on Ukraine, while the US is trying to make deals with Russia over its diesel and lift sanctions. Russia keeps striking Ukraine’s energy system and cities, while its drones and suspected saboteurs keep turning up inside NATO, from tankers hit off Romania to a foiled arson attempt at a Starlink site in Lithuania.
Down within minutes
The F-16s took off from the 86th Air Base at Borcea at 17:43 after radar detected a group of air targets about 120 km east of Zmiinyi (Snake) Island, flying southwest, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported, citing the ministry. The first drone entered Romanian airspace at 17:59 and was shot down at 18:01 southeast of Sulina. The second entered at 18:01 and was downed at 18:05 east of Sulina.
Both were jet-powered attack drones of the Geran family, the ministry said. The Geran is Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed. When first detected, the drones were about 65 km from the coast of Russian-occupied Crimea and 140 km from the Ukrainian-held shore, and their southwest course may point to Russian origin, Militarnyi calculated.
Congress gave Trump 30 days to hit Russia’s oil buyers with 100% tariffs. He waives them two days before deadline, citing US interests. Moscow calls it historic
The ministry posted the cockpit images on 18 October, showing a missile launch and a fireball over the sea. “Targets spotted, identified, engaged and neutralized!” it wrote.
Allies to meet on the Black Sea
A special session of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s top decision-making body, will discuss defense and deterrence in the Black Sea on 20 October at Romania’s request. Romanian President Nicușor Dan has confirmed that the two tankers that caught fire near Sulina last week were hit by drones, and a NATO military source told Reuters they were Russian.
Romanian radar has logged 54 drone intrusions into the country’s air and sea space since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 35 of them this year, and the military has shot down six such targets in 2026, Defense Ministry data show.
Searches in Poland and Lithuania
Within hours, Poland’s Operational Command said it was checking a possible airspace violation by an unknown object overnight into 18 October. Troops, police, and military police searched for a possible crash site south of Lublin after residents reported the loud sound of a flying object around 02:00, Militarnyi reported.
On the morning of 18 October, an unknown drone entered Lithuania’s airspace and triggered air raid alerts, the country’s crisis management center said. NATO jets accompanied it but could not shoot it down because of bad weather, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said. Debris preliminarily identified as drone parts was later found in the village of Juodžioniai in Pasvalys district, and the army said the drone may have entered from the direction of Poland.
Romania moved from escorting Russia’s stray drones to firing on them in July, when its F-16s downed three in 72 hours.
