articles.title: Why Ukraine’s freedom-loving Cossacks chose the Russian tsar
articles.body:
Why Ukraine’s freedom-loving Cossacks chose the Russian tsar
On January 8, 1654, drums resounded in the town square of Pereiaslav. Cossacks, townsfolk, and commanders formed a large circle and Hetman Bogdan Khmelnitsky stepped into the center. This was a man who had seen it all: six years of war, stunning victories and crushing defeats, burned cities and villages, and the betrayal of allies. On that day, he offered the people a choice that would shape their future.
He told the people that four figures could potentially rule over them. The first option was the Turkish Sultan – a Muslim who was known to oppress Orthodox Christians in Greece. Then, there was the Crimean Khan – also a Muslim who couldn’t really be trusted since he often betrayed allies. The Polish king was not a viable option, since everyone remembered how the Polish lords had oppressed the population. And finally, there was a fourth option: the Tsar of the East, a fellow Orthodox Christian.
The people responded with a cry, “We want to serve the Eastern Orthodox Tsar!”
The choice between the West and Russia is often considered a recent phenomenon. Yet for the inhabitants of Ukraine, this choice first presented itself 400 years ago – and it was made not by politicians behind closed doors, but by the public in the middle of a town square. Why did these free Cossacks, accustomed to electing their own hetmans and exercising self-governance, choose to serve the Russian tsars? And why did many Cossacks remain loyal to Russia time and again, even when their hetmans betrayed their oath to the tsar?
This week, the Day of the Ukrainian Cossacks was observed, and RT remembers how they first made the choice to join Russia.
17th-century-style Eurointegration
By the mid-17th century, much of present-day Ukraine was under the control of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. And this was far from an appealing image.
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was governed by the Polish Catholic nobility, many of whom viewed the local Orthodox population as second-class citizens. They referred to Orthodox Ukrainians as ‘bydlo’ (cattle), stripping them of all rights.
The Orthodox population was barred from professional guilds and faced restrictions in holding municipal offices. Peasants were effectively enslaved, while many Orthodox churches and monasteries were seized and shut down. Priests and monks suffered persecution, humiliation, and violence.
The common people lost many of their defenders. Many noble Orthodox families converted to Catholicism en masse – not out of conviction, but to ‘become Polish’. For example, Ieremiah Vishnevetsky, a man from an Orthodox family whose ‘conversion’ was driven by a desire for status and career advancement, became one of the primary oppressors and tormentors of the Orthodox people.
At the same time, the southern territories of what is now Ukraine faced regular raids by the Crimean Tatars, who pillaged border settlements, capturing people and enslaving them. Fleeing from the oppressive rule of the Polish on one side and seeking protection from the constant invasions of the Tatars on the other, Ukraine’s Orthodox population retreated into the so-called Wild Field. In the expansive, fertile steppes stretching from the Dniester to the Don rivers, there was no authority to govern them. These people established their own communities and formed self-defense groups; they became known as Cossacks. Living on the frontier, in conditions far harsher than those of America’s Wild West, they always had their weapons at hand.
The Cossacks launched campaigns against the Crimean Khanate and the Ottoman Empire, but their primary focus was on preserving their Orthodox faith and resisting Polish oppression. Throughout the first half of the 17th century, uprisings frequently erupted across Ukraine, but due to the Cossacks’ poor organization and the superior military training of the Poles, these rebellions were consistently crushed with brutal force.
By 1648, it seemed that the Poles had eradicated all the rebellious Cossacks and subjugated the populace. For the Polish, it seemed like there was nothing more to worry about. However, this was a grave mistake.
Unity of faith
Against the background of the horrifying national and religious oppression raging in Ukraine, the neighboring Orthodox Russian Tsardom presented a stark contrast. At the beginning of the 17th century, Russia had endured a brutal civil war and foreign intervention known as the Time of Troubles. Nevertheless, it had managed to repel external foes and was steadily regaining its strength. This powerful, centralized Orthodox state naturally drew the attention of the Cossacks.
During this period, identity was largely defined by faith, and the terms ‘Orthodox’ and ‘Russian’ were nearly interchangeable. At that time, there was no clear distinction between Russians and Ukrainians; both identified as Russian, viewing themselves as heirs to the medieval state of Kievan Rus’.
While people in the Russian Tsardom and modern-day Ukraine had their linguistic and regional differences, they had a lot more in common with each other than with the Poles. National and religious identities were intertwined, which is why Cossack leader Bogdan Khmelnitsky, in his speech at the Pereiaslav Council emphasized this unity by saying, “We share the same faith.”
However, a shared faith and identity didn’t automatically translate into political decisions. Whenever uprisings happened, Cossack delegations went to Moscow seeking assistance. In 1620, Cossack Hetman Pyotr Sagaidachny wrote to Tsar Mikhail Fyodorovich, expressing the Cossacks’ readiness to serve him. In 1624, Metropolitan Iov Boretsky of Kiev directly appealed to the Russian tsar, asking him to protect the “brotherly people” and to incorporate Malorossiya (literally, Little Russia – one of Ukraine’s historical names) into Russia. But at the beginning of the 17th century, Russia was just recovering from the turmoil of the Time of Troubles and was not prepared for a new war with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, so it responded to these appeals with caution.
Nonetheless, this did not deter the people of modern-day Ukraine. In the 1630s, thousands of Cossacks migrated to the Russian Tsardom, settling along its southern borders. After the defeat of the 1638 uprising, Hetman Yakov Ostrianin led 1,000 Cossacks and their families into Russia. He settled in Chuguev (present-day Kharkov region), where the tsarist government was constructing a new fortress, and helped repel Tatar raids on the southern frontiers alongside Russian troops. Thus, the historical region known as Slobozhanshchina emerged, which encompassed the modern-day Ukrainian cities of Sumy, Kharkov, Izium, and others. Cossacks who served the Tsar settled there, living next to the Russian forces that were stationed in the area.
Ultimately, the unity between the Russian Tsardom and Orthodox Ukrainians was sealed by Bogdan Khmelnitsky.
Free choice
Bogdan Khmelnitsky knew from personal experience the futility of seeking peaceful and respectful relations with the Poles. By age 50, he had a successful military career, numerous campaigns, and years of loyal service to the Polish king behind his back. In 1648, he held the rank of Cossack hundredman (similar to a company commander) in Chigirin. However, taking advantage of Khmelnitsky’s absence, the nobleman Chaplinsky seized his family estate, kidnapped his wife, and assaulted (or, according to some reports, killed) his son. When Khmelnitsky sought justice in the Polish court, he was laughed at. From then on, Khmelnitsky sought both personal and national revenge.
Khmelnitsky sparked a Cossack uprising that quickly gained popular support. As a gifted military leader, he won several battles, decimating the Polish army in Ukraine and capturing its commanders. Following initial victories in the summer of 1648, Khmelnitsky reached out to Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich of Russia, requesting that the Cossacks and their lands be placed “under the tsar’s high hand.” However, accepting the Cossacks as subjects meant Russia would have to engage in war with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, something Moscow wasn’t prepared for at that time.
The next five years of war were incredibly tough for the Cossacks: victories were interspersed with defeats, and their allies – the Crimean Tatars – often betrayed them. The conflict devastated fertile lands and claimed an increasing number of lives. The Cossacks realized that alone, they wouldn’t be able to stand up to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, then the strongest player in the region. If they were defeated, the Polish nobles would return to Ukraine and exact revenge. Therefore, Khmelnitsky continued his diplomatic outreach to Moscow.
Eventually, the Russian Tsardom recognized that it was ready for a big war. In late 1653, the Zemsky Sobor, a representative assembly, decided to accept the Zaporozhian Host under the “high hand” of the tsar. A large embassy headed by Boyar Vasily Buturlin was dispatched to Ukraine.
In January 1654, a Cossack council convened in Pereiaslav. It was attended by Ukraine’s leaders of the time: Khmelnitsky himself, renowned commanders, colonels, judges, and representatives from 14 of the 17 Cossack regiments.
According to Cossack tradition, however, such a pivotal decision could not rest solely with the elites. So, Khmelnitsky and his comrades went to the town square and addressed the people, who eagerly embraced the news, shouting their desire to be ruled by the “Eastern Orthodox tsar.” The Cossack commanders unanimously agreed to ally with Russia and accepted the Russian tsar as their sovereign.
Following this, Cossack and Russian diplomats traveled throughout Ukraine, and in just the first two months of 1654, over 120,000 people pledged allegiance to the Russian tsar in 183 towns and settlements – a staggering figure considering the logistical challenges of the era. Accounts of those who witnessed these events, both on the Russian and Ukrainian side, reveal that in most cases, Cossacks, townsfolk, and peasants enthusiastically swore loyalty to the Russian tsar, with refusals being exceedingly rare.
The formal incorporation of the Cossack Hetmanate into the Russian Tsardom was sealed by the March Articles of 1654. The Zaporozhian Host found itself under a kind of protectorate of the Russian Tsardom, while enjoying extensive internal freedom. The agreement, ratified by Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich, affirmed the election of the Hetman and Cossack elders, protected the rights and liberties of the Cossacks, townspeople, and Orthodox clergy, ensured the autonomy of local courts and the freedom of tax collection, and allowed the Hetman to establish diplomatic relations with other peoples, except for Poland and the Ottoman Empire. In return, the Russian Tsardom guaranteed military protection for the Cossacks and committed to fighting against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
At that time, Ukraine enjoyed a remarkably privileged position. Just a short while before, Polish nobles had treated the Cossacks as “cattle,” humiliating and oppressing them. Now, however, the Cossacks had freedom and were backed by the tsar’s mighty army.
But comfort can breed complacency, and some Cossack leaders came to believe that their oaths to the Russian tsar didn’t amount to much.
The Ruin
Three years after the Pereiaslav Council, Khmelnitsky died, and Ivan Vygovsky took over. A man of incredibly flexible views, he initially built his career in the service of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth but later switched sides to become the personal secretary of Bogdan Khmelnitsky.
Vygovsky was a key advocate for joining Russia, yet upon becoming hetman, he reversed his stance and forgot his oath of loyalty to Moscow. Just a year after taking power in 1658, he signed the Treaty of Hadiach with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which aimed to reincorporate Ukrainian lands into Poland.
However, it soon became apparent that the decision of 1654 wasn’t made solely by the Cossack leadership. Early on, at the stage of negotiations with Poland, figures like Colonel Martyn Pushkar and Zaporozhian Otaman Yakov Barabash opposed the decision to defect to the Polish side and betray their Orthodox brethren. Many Cossacks and townsfolk rallied behind them. For these individuals, returning to Polish rule meant a return to oppression and humiliation. Vygovsky managed to suppress this particular uprising, and commanders loyal to Russia were killed.
After Vygovsky’s open betrayal, however, many prominent Cossack leaders – including those now celebrated as Ukrainian national heroes, such as Ivan Bogun and Ivan Sirko – rose against him. For them, as for the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians at the time, treason against the Russian tsar and submission to the Polish were intolerable.
Consequently, the Cossacks united with Russian forces against the traitors. Notably, in 1658, Kiev was defended from Vygovsky’s troops by the combined forces of Tsarist voivode Vasily Sheremetev and Kiev colonel Vasily Dvoretsky. As the conflict escalated, not only Cossacks but even townspeople and ordinary peasants turned against Vygovsky’s allies. Those who had betrayed their oath to the tsar were often punished or killed by the people.
Pro-Russian Cossacks and Tsarist troops united to inflict a series of defeats upon Vygovsky; he lost power and fled to Poland, where he was ultimately executed without trial, since he was no longer needed. This stands in stark contrast to Dvoretsky, whose descendants remained influential members of the local Malorossian elite until 1917.
This story illustrated that Russia’s influence in Ukraine rested not on fleeting decisions made by individual commanders but on the overwhelming support of the populace. However, at that point, Ukraine plunged into decades of civil strife.
In 1659, Yuriy Khmelnitsky, the son of Bogdan Khmelnitsky, became hetman and signed new agreements with Russia. By then, Russia had begun to grasp the unique political culture of the Ukrainian elites and started to curb Cossack independence. Under the new terms, electing a hetman or making international decisions required the tsar’s approval, and the presence of Russian garrisons increased in Ukrainian cities.
However, soon after signing the treaty with Moscow, Yuriy Khmelnitsky launched a war against the Poles. Having lost this war, he ended up signing another agreement with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
Yet another Cossack hetman had ‘outplayed’ himself, negotiating worse terms with the Poles than with the Russians. As a result, Cossack autonomy was curbed and they were obligated to fight alongside the Poles against the Russian Tsardom.
The Cossack regiments stationed on the eastern bank of the Dnieper river rejected this betrayal, leading to a de facto split of Ukraine into Left and Right Banks. This marked the beginning of Ukraine’s own ‘game of thrones’. Subsequent hetmans and atamans followed a familiar pattern: from declarations of loyalty to Russia to restrictions on Cossack autonomy; from formal allegiance to betrayal and eventual death or exile.
Russia managed to put an end to this chaotic cycle of conflict only by signing the Truce of Andrusovo with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1667, which divided Ukraine along the Dnieper River.
Mazepa’s betrayal and the people’s loyalty
One of the most dramatic tests of the Cossacks’ loyalty to Russia unfolded during the Great Northern War. Russia was fighting Sweden for access to the Baltic Sea, as Sweden was the dominant power in Northern Europe at the time. In the early years, the war proved challenging for Russia, prompting Hetman Ivan Mazepa, who had been in power for over 20 years, to betray his old ally, Tsar Peter the Great, and ally himself with Swedish King Charles XII (whom he believed would emerge as the victor).
In the summer of 1708, General Judge Vasily Kochubey and Colonel Ivan Iskra reported Mazepa’s secret contacts with the Swedes. However, Peter the Great trusted his old friend so much that he dismissed their warnings. Kochubey and Iskra were executed, but once Mazepa’s treachery came to light, they were posthumously rehabilitated; the Kochubey family later received a noble title and several military and state leaders of the Russian Empire were descended from it.
In late autumn 1708, Mazepa finally defected to Charles XII’s side. Notably, only a few thousand people followed him. When it became clear that this was not merely a campaign but outright betrayal, the ranks of Mazepa’s supporters dwindled even further.
The vast majority of Cossacks remained loyal to Russia. They fought alongside Russian troops against the Swedes. Being Orthodox Christians, they could not fathom the idea of siding with the enemies who were, moreover, Protestants. Similarly, ordinary townspeople and peasants stayed true to Russia.
In his first address to the Cossacks, the new hetman Ivan Skoropadsky asserted that “All of Ukraine must be loyal to Moscow, and must not be seduced by the friendship of the Swedes, who, aside from being entirely foreign to Ukraine, are not even neighbors.”
Modern Ukrainian historians tend to romanticize Mazepa as a champion of freedom and independence, but this portrayal is misleading. Mazepa and his circle were simply looking for a new master, driven by a false sense of Russia’s vulnerability. In reality, the people of Ukraine remained steadfastly loyal to Russia and the Orthodox Tsar, with Cossack regiments fighting side by side with tsarist forces during the legendary Battle of Poltava.
From maces to ministerial positions
Following Mazepa’s betrayal, Russia systematically curtailed Cossack autonomy. Despite the unwavering loyalty of the vast majority of Cossacks, the treachery of their leaders became increasingly audacious. In 1722, Peter the Great established the Collegium of Little Russia, essentially a ministry for Ukrainian affairs.
The position of hetman was alternately abolished and reinstated, but the Cossacks’ autonomy was steadily curbed. Those who failed to grasp that times had changed, like the appointed hetman Pavel Polubotok, found themselves imprisoned in the Peter and Paul Fortress.
Concurrently, another trend emerged. Cossack leaders began integrating into the imperial elite, a shift that, for many of them, proved more beneficial than the semblance of freedom.
Alexei Razumovsky, the son of a humble Cossack, arrived in St. Petersburg as a singer in the court chapel and eventually became the favorite (and according to some accounts, the secret husband) of Empress Elizabeth. His brother, Kirill, headed the Russian Academy of Sciences and served as the last hetman. Alexander Bezborodko, the son of a general scribe, rose to become Chancellor of the Russian Empire. Pyotr Zavadovsky became the first Minister of Public Education in Russia. Victor Kochubey, a descendant of the executed judge, served as Minister of Internal Affairs and Chairman of the State Council of the Russian Empire. The list of the descendants of the Cossacks who achieved high office in the Russian Empire goes on and on.
The era of the Cossacks eventually faded into history.
In 1764, Razumovsky laid down his mace. Cossack regiments were transformed into regular hussar and carabiner regiments. The Charter of 1785 equalized the rights of Cossack leaders with those of the Russian nobility.
A century and a half earlier, in 1648, the Cossacks had launched a rebellion against the Poles, fighting for their own rights, laws, and the Orthodox faith. In 1654, they pledged allegiance to the Russian Tsar in Pereiaslav. Later on, many events unfolded: the Cossacks oscillated between Poland, Turkey, and Sweden, yet the majority remained loyal to Russia.
There were numerous reasons for this loyalty. A shared identity and faith made rapprochement with Moscow natural; fear of foreign lords, khans, and sultans united the Cossacks under Russian banners. Moreover, social interests and career aspirations made serving the empire appealing. Some were driven by sincere motives; others acted out of fear or personal gain.
Ultimately, those who remained loyal to the Orthodox Russian Tsar emerged as the winners, exchanging their former unprivileged status for the right to build the empire alongside the Russians.

articles.title: Rubio explains why Trump waived sanctions against Russia, says administration needs time to assess impact
articles.body:
Rubio explains why Trump waived sanctions against Russia, says administration needs time to assess impact
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that President Donald Trump had signed an executive order waiving the imposition of sanctions against Russia under the Graham Act for 60 days to assess how they might affect the US and global economies.
Source: Marco Rubio speaking to journalists, as reported by European Pravda
Quote: "The problem is these sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries – India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy.
I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this, given all the different things that are going on in the world right now, including the pressure on global energy supplies."
Details: Rubio said that global energy prices have been affected not only by the situation in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, but also by Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and, supposedly, the war between Russia and Ukraine, "where energy infrastructure is being hit".
He noted that the administration needs 60 days to "take all of that into account and weigh it against each other".
Rubio cited India as an example, saying that the country has voluntarily diversified its supplies but still obtains a significant share of its energy resources from Russia.
When asked by a journalist whether the decision amounts to a gift to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, the secretary of state said Russian diesel fuel "was going to be sold one way or the other".
Quote: "The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they will make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get. But this is not unprecedented. If you recall, a few months ago, we also did a 60-day waiver on Russian oil when Hormuz was being challenged."
Details: Rubio noted that conflicts around the world are now interconnected and could therefore create uncertainty in global energy markets.
"So all of these things have to be managed delicately because they're all coming together now. It's not just the Strait of Hormuz anymore. It's what's happening with Saudi Arabia and the uncertainty that that's creating. It's also what's happening between Russia and Ukraine and the constraints that's putting on global energy supplies," he added.
Background:
- On 16 October, Trump signed an executive order waiving the application of sanctions against Russia under the Graham Act. He said the decision was in the US national interest. The deadline for Trump to impose new sanctions on Russia expires on 18 October.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Graham Act could still put pressure on Russia despite Trump's decision not to introduce new restrictions under it for the time being.
- Senator Richard Blumenthal, who helped draft the Graham Act, sharply criticised Trump for refusing to take further steps to put pressure on Russia under the law.

articles.title: Iran to answer 'mother of all bombs' with 'father of bombs': senior IRGC commander
articles.body:
Iran to answer 'mother of all bombs' with 'father of bombs': senior IRGC commander
TEHRAN – Deputy Coordinator of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps, Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Naqdi, has warned the United States against any military miscalculation against Iran, saying Tehran would respond to Washington's "mother of all bombs" with the "father of bombs."
Speaking on Sunday afternoon at the "Self-Sacrificers for Iran" rally in Sari, Naqdi was referring to recent threats by US President Donald Trump to use the GBU-43/B massive ordnance, widely known as the mother of all bombs, against Iran.
"If you make a wrong move, we will come for you with the father of bombs, and all your assets will be at risk," Naqdi said.
He described Trump's remarks as a sign of fatigue and depleted patience in confronting a nation that resists pressure, arguing that the threats reflect the difficulty of dealing with Iran.
Criticizing the threats to use heavy bombs, Naqdi said the enemy had already used heavy weaponry in the past, but those actions had failed to achieve US objectives. He also claimed that parts of the technology used in some of the weapons deployed against Iran are now in the hands of Iranian forces and are under examination.
Warning of the consequences of any military action, he said any miscalculation and escalation could jeopardize the security of US investments and economic activities in the region, including American technology, artificial intelligence and oil companies operating in the region.
On Iran's deterrent power, Naqdi said the country's defense capability in land and naval domains is not limited to military hardware alone, stressing that the will of a people who stand to defend their land is a key element of that power.
"The enemy may be able to take certain actions, but the fundamental question is whether it can achieve its goals. Our defensive readiness and the will of the Iranian people have complicated the enemy's calculations," he said.
He added that US military movements in the region have been affected by Iran's defense capabilities.
Naqdi said such threats may pursue different objectives, including creating division among the people, weakening the resolve of officials and reducing the readiness of the Armed Forces. He stressed the need to preserve national unity, stay vigilant against psychological warfare, and prevent internal disputes.
Maintaining the country's defense preparedness, solidarity between the people and officials, and cohesion of the Armed Forces play a decisive role in countering foreign threats, he said, adding that threats should not cause any doubt in defending national interests.

articles.title: U.S. resumes intelligence sharing with Ukraine – Zelensky
articles.body:
U.S. resumes intelligence sharing with Ukraine – Zelensky
As reported by Ukrinform, Zelensky said this during an appearance on Meet the Press on NBC News.
“We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” he said.
Zelensky told moderator Kristen Welker that, in the view of Ukrainian officials, SpaceX’s decision to restrict the operation of Elon Musk’s Starlink system was a response to a “message from American government.”
Commenting on President Donald Trump’s statement earlier this week that the Ukrainian leader was “more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Zelensky said he had been “very hones” in his dealings with Trump.
“Maybe it’s not very polite,” he said, but it is “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.”
Zelensky warned that President Trump’s agreement with Russia on diesel fuel supplies “will strengthen Putin in his will to occupy us.”
Announcing the agreement, Trump expressed hope that it would help address the sharp rise in fuel prices to some extent.
Zelensky, however, noted that the agreement wouldn’t have “a real influence” on oil prices in the United States, as the increase was caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz rather than the situation in Ukraine.
“I don’t know all the reasons why President Trump makes such deals,” he said.
As reported by Ukrinform, with U.S. approval, Russia will immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel to the global market and significantly increase its exports going forward.

articles.title: Russia’s war in Ukraine puts Europe on edge
articles.body:
Talk to Al Jazeera
Russia’s war in Ukraine puts Europe on edge
Fears are growing that Russia’s war in Ukraine could spill over into neighbouring NATO members – and spread regionally.
Some countries would argue it already has – pointing to drone incursions, cyberattacks and sabotage.
European nations say Moscow is targeting Ukraine’s allies to intimidate them. The Kremlin denies the accusations.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warns Europe should be ready to respond robustly to Russia’s hybrid attacks.
Poland, which borders Ukraine, is home to a NATO logistics hub used for military and civilian support to its neighbour.
The International Centre for Counterterrorism says the country is the ‘primary focus’ of Russia’s sabotage campaign in Europe.
It’s also the country most targeted by cyberattacks, according to research from Harvard, with about four thousand politically motivated attacks per day.
And Poland is on heightened alert.
It’s reported several airspace violations — and authorities say more drone and missile strikes are likely.
Sikorski says that for the war to end Russian President Vladimir Putin would have to admit his original goals are unachievable and that the full-scale invasion of Ukraine was a mistake.

articles.title: St. Petersburg oil site burns as 1,000 Ukrainian drones bite Russia
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone strikes set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest aerial bombardments to date.
The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington , with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
One person was killed and five more were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at both the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, said local Gov. Alexander Beglov.
A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center for local tech giant VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.
Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agnecy Tass that Kyiv was "resisting" Moscow's invasion, but that Ukraine could not "change the current course of events."
Meanwhile, a woman died and at least two other people were wounded, including a 6-year-old girl, after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said.
Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged as a result of the attack, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin said.
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy cease-fire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Ukraine confirmed Thursday it had resumed attacks on Russian oil after a three-day hiatus.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government initially said that it was heeding the cease-fire.
In a post on X Sunday, Zelenskyy said that in the week since Trump’s announcement of an energy cease-fire, Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times.
He also said that in the past night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," he wrote.
Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia’s invasion – not because Ukraine was defending itself.
"It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps," he said.
Trump told reporters Saturday that they don’t know what his decision is yet regarding further sanctions on Russia, despite the executive order he signed Friday night waiving planned restrictions, citing a U.S. national interest.
"We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out. But it’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world," Trump said at a fundraising dinner at his Florida estate.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Newest TOS-3 Dragon Thermobaric Rocket Launcher for First Time, Video
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Newest TOS-3 Dragon Thermobaric Rocket Launcher for First Time, Video
Ukrainian forces have struck Russia’s newest TOS-3 “Dragon” heavy flamethrower system for the first time, using a drone to target the tracked thermobaric rocket launcher approximately 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) behind the front line.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Third Army Corps on October 17, the strike was carried out by operators of the Muramasa unit, part of the Kraken Unmanned Systems Regiment, during the ongoing offensive operation known as “Vivaldi.”
The Ukrainian military said the Russian launcher was identified after it had conducted a firing mission. Drone operators subsequently located and struck the system, with footage of the engagement released through the corps’ official channels.
The Third Army Corps described the attack as the first reported successful strike against the TOS-3, a recently developed Russian weapon designed to deliver thermobaric rockets against fortified positions and concentrations of troops.
The TOS-3 “Dragon” is the latest addition to Russia’s family of heavy flamethrower systems, following the TOS-1A “Solntsepyok” and TOS-2 “Tosochka.”
Unlike the wheeled TOS-2, the TOS-3 uses a tracked, tank-type chassis intended to improve mobility across difficult terrain while providing greater protection for its crew.
According to specifications shared by the Third Army Corps, the launcher carries 15 tubes for unguided thermobaric rockets and has an estimated firing range of up to 15 kilometers (9.3 miles).
The system is operated by a three-person crew and incorporates additional protective measures, including slat armor and explosive reactive armor intended to improve its survivability against incoming attacks.
Thermobaric weapons use explosive mixtures that generate intense heat and prolonged blast pressure, making them particularly destructive against enclosed positions, trenches, and fortified structures.
The reported strike took place during Operation Vivaldi, an offensive campaign conducted by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps in the northern part of the Donetsk region.
During the same operation, Ukrainian forces deployed unmanned ground vehicles behind Russian positions, contributing to the liberation of two villages and the clearing of another settlement.
Ukrainian units also adapted ground-based attack drones with grenade launchers to engage Russian positions, demonstrating the expanding use of unmanned systems in offensive operations.

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Railway Bridge in Bryansk, Blasts Military Supply Depots Across Donetsk
Ukrainian forces struck a railway bridge in Russia’s Bryansk region and several Russian military logistics facilities in temporarily occupied Donetsk region during operations conducted on October 16 and overnight into October 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 17, the strikes targeted infrastructure used by Russian forces to transport military supplies, store equipment, and coordinate drone operations.
One of the targets was a railway bridge spanning the Unecha River near Sloboda-Seletskaya in Russia’s Bryansk region. Ukrainian military officials confirmed that the bridge had been hit but did not specify the extent of the damage.
The railway crossing is part of the transport infrastructure that can be used to move military cargo. Disrupting such routes could complicate Russian efforts to deliver ammunition, fuel, and military equipment to its forces operating in Ukraine.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck Russian military supply depots in three locations across temporarily occupied Donetsk region.
The General Staff identified the areas near Novoandriivka, Nikolske, and Mariupol as the locations of the attacks. The facilities were reportedly used to store logistical supplies supporting Russian military operations.
Another strike targeted a Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) command post near Malynivka in Donetsk region. The Ukrainian military did not disclose the type of weapons used or provide an assessment of Russian equipment losses.
Earlier, on October 16, Ukrainian forces targeted a second Russian Mi-28NM attack helicopter in less than a week using a domestically produced VB140 Flamingo interceptor drone over Russia’s Belgorod region. Footage released by Ukraine’s 115th Separate Mechanized Brigade showed the drone approaching the helicopter, although the extent of any damage remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: The language of extermination: NAZA, Artificial Intelligence and Gaza
articles.body:
The 80-minute documentary NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is chastening. It examines the conduct of the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) during its ferocious, unremitting war in Gaza, drawing upon the interviews of 24 anonymised military and intelligence personnel. The interviews were filmed on Tel Aviv rooftops at night, with profiles and voices appropriately altered. The name of the documentary draws on a Hebrew acronym for nezek agavi or collateral damage, an obscene term used when counting the estimated number of civilians who will perish in a military strike. Last month, the film won the Special Jury Prize at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, receiving a standing ovation lasting 25 minutes.
The interviewees focus on the terrifyingly relevant role played by Artificial Intelligence (AI) targeting systems used in guiding the bombing campaign launched in response to the Hamas-led attacks of 7th October 2023. In Abraham’s words, “the Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us about how this mass killing is systemic: not by accident, but by design, actions of murder and policies that are based on the total dehumanisation of Palestinians.”
One of the interviewed subjects speaks of the goal being “quantity, not quality.” Another notes the conscious decision to target Hamas members, some even in the lower echelons, when they would be at home even if it meant killing family members and neighbours.
In one recalled instance, the phone of a 12-year-old girl was hacked to learn when her father would arrive home. The subsequent strike killed her. The cold logic is revealed in the rhetorical question posed by one of the interviewees: “When people talk about ‘flattening Gaza,’ what do you mean if not executing people?’
Despite being placed in a “too hot to handle” category by prominent indie studios, the self-distributed documentary managed to pass the US$500,000 mark in the United States after two weeks of release. Eight days after premiering at New York’s IFC Center, it went on to earn US$125,000. A further 85 theatres across 30 cities across North America then showed the film. Michelle Goldberg, writing in The New York Times, was impressed by the drawing power of the production when attending Walter Reade Theater for a screening. The venue, seating 268, was at capacity. “This is, in my experience, very unusual for documentaries of any sort, even those that, like ‘NAZA,’ win the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.”
Militaries specialise in euphemised killing. A dedicated process of terminology and assessment sanitises and exsanguinates: death and murder become justifiable, necessary measures against an enemy bloated with wickedness and venality. In that process, mock tributes are paid to the canon of international law, notably international humanitarian law and doctrines of targeting. The more honest generals do us a favour by boasting about high casualty figures and mass mortality: they are not hiding matters and lurking behind worn ceremonies and the emperor’s non-existent clothes. Take the remarks of a former head of Israeli military intelligence made in a leaked audio: “For every one person [killed] on Oct. 7, 50 Palestinians must die.” Those militaries with a heavily staffed legal department supposedly providing guidance in striking a target, largely to reassure the squeamish that they are not implicated in acts of murder, are always suspect. In that regard, the IDF provides a model example, always claiming to do things differently from other powers in the region, yet resorting to the selective language of exculpation.
The reception of the film in Israel has been markedly hysterical. This was to be expected: the film unmasks and discomfits. It demolishes shibboleths. The IDF chief of staff Eyal Zamir vowed to use “every tool at our disposal” against the production. The Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar thought the film treasonous.
Abraham and Szor were “willing to harm their homeland in order just to get applause from antisemites around the world”. The irate minister was keen to “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” he thundered in a social media post. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also called upon the passing of legislation stripping the duo of their citizenship, a curious point given the existing provisions of Israel’s Citizenship Law. (Making German Jews stateless was a specialty of the Third Reich: that the Jewish state would consider this to its citizens is a distinct, bitter irony, yet sadly permissible in light of the Israeli Supreme Court ruling in 2022 validating revocation for acts done in “breach of loyalty to the State of Israel”.)
Activists and members of the far-right party Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir protested outside the parents of Szor’s house, with a speaker calling for both directors to be executed and the homes of their families to be demolished (collective punishment remains a great inspiration for tribal sentiment).
The IDF has marshalled its own response in a document accusing the filmmakers of presenting “a distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture of the IDF’s target planning and striking process.” The narrative of the documentary drew upon “substantial factual errors stemming from manipulative misrepresentations of reality.” Worth noting here is the lower register of critique that does not entirely repudiate the targeting practices of the IDF, dressed up in the apologetics of collateral damage. Concessions and confessions are always evident from those in and of power who resort to such dismissive language as “misrepresentative” and “disingenuous”.
Be that as it may, the agitated response is illuminating. The Lavender database, to take one objection, was apparently not one of targets, merely “a database that assists intelligence analysts.” This represents a distinction without a difference. The faith placed by militaries in the divinities of technology are hard to shake; there is nothing here to say that such analysts do not treat these data sets as unimpeachable. AI and religious deities serve to do the imagination for others; they discourage independent thinking and verification. Why bother when you have someone, or something else, doing it for you?
The response remains weak in claiming that the IDF believes itself “bound by and committed to international humanitarian law, its operational procedures are designed to implement those legal obligations, and it operates dedicated units and mechanisms to mitigate civilian harm.” The staggering death toll in Gaza, always sneered and jeered at by the Israeli authorities and their defenders, would suggest otherwise.
NAZA serves to, as the Israeli American historian Omer Bartov points out, address a “state of denial” by “actually speaking about the issue of what happened in Gaza rather than refusing to speak about it.”

articles.title: Before there is nothing left to save
articles.body:
Before there is nothing left to save
There are mornings in wartime when the silence itself seems wounded.
The roads are still there, though fewer people travel them. The fields remain beneath the grey sky, though in places they are scarred by fire. Somewhere a railway station opens its doors, a baker lights an oven, a woman draws back a curtain – and for a moment life pretends that it has not been broken.
But the war goes on. And whenever a new round of negotiations, with American representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner taking part, ends with cautiously hopeful words from Moscow describing them as progressive and encouraging, Vladimir Zelensky later returns to the hard, uncompromising tone that has become familiar throughout these years.
Listening to him, one is left with a painful question.
Does he still believe that peace can be reached only through continued resistance, whatever the cost? Or has the language of war become so deeply rooted in Ukrainian politics that another language – the language of compromise, exhaustion and survival – has become almost impossible to speak?
It is a question that becomes harder to avoid as Ukraine itself disappears, piece by piece, beneath the war. The destruction continues tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow.
Ukraine has inflicted damage on Russia too. Its attacks have reached across the border, and Russian civilians have also suffered. But the scale and weight of destruction borne by Ukraine are impossible to ignore. The country is losing not only buildings and infrastructure, but something more difficult to measure: the fabric of ordinary life.
There are also reports of bitter internal struggles within the Ukrainian government. Zelensky’s former press secretary spoke recently of constant fighting at different levels of government.
War is dangerous enough when an enemy stands beyond the border. It becomes still more dangerous when a nation begins to quarrel with itself.
This is why any negotiations deserve attention. Perhaps they will fail. Perhaps the words spoken around the negotiating table will evaporate like mist over a river. Perhaps the armies will return to the battlefield and the familiar language of missiles, trenches and casualties will once again drown out every other voice. But negotiations, however imperfect, are preferable to another year of graves.
There is a moment in every long war when the question changes.
At first, people ask: How can we win?
Later they begin to ask: How much will victory cost?
And finally, sometimes very quietly, they ask the question that frightened leaders are reluctant to hear:
What will be left of us when the fighting stops?
Ukraine has received enormous support from its Western allies. Much of that support has been born of genuine sympathy and a desire to defend Ukrainian sovereignty. But Western governments also have their own histories, strategic interests and grievances concerning Russia – grievances that reach back decades.
That is the nature of international politics.
But Ukraine is not a chessboard.
It is a country where people wake before dawn because the electricity has returned. It is a mother waiting for a message from her son. It is an empty chair at a family table. It is an orchard in spring, flowering while artillery is heard somewhere beyond the horizon.
Those who advise Ukraine from comfortable offices far away will return home when the meeting is over.
Ukrainians cannot.
They will remain among the ruins.
Perhaps Zelensky should now listen not only to those who tell him how long Ukraine can continue fighting, but also to those who ask how long Ukraine can continue being destroyed.
Perhaps the future will demand compromises that today seem unbearable.
Perhaps Ukraine will never enter NATO in the way some once imagined. Perhaps membership of the European Union will remain a distant horizon rather than an immediate destination. Perhaps some political ambitions will have to wait for another generation.
History does not always give nations the future they desire. Sometimes it gives them only the future they can still preserve. There is nothing shameful in recognizing that.
Peace is not always a reward for victory. Sometimes it is an act of courage undertaken before victory becomes indistinguishable from ruin.
A leader must know when to fight. But a leader must also know when to stop.
The most dangerous words in wartime are sometimes not the words of the enemy. They are the words that tell a wounded nation that tomorrow will always be better than today if only it sacrifices a little more.
There is always another hill. Another offensive. Another shipment of weapons. Another season. And then another grave. At some point, someone has to look at the country itself.
Not at the speeches. Not at the flags. Not at the photographs of leaders standing before cameras, solemn and determined. At the country. At its empty villages. At its shattered cities. At its railway lines disappearing into the distance. At the blackened windows where, once, there were lights.
A country is not its government. It is not its president. It is not an alliance or a treaty. A country is the people who remain. And perhaps this is the moment when Zelensky must ask himself the simplest and hardest question of all:
How much of Ukraine must be destroyed before the world admits that saving Ukraine has to come before defeating Russia?
There is still time to ask it. But time, like everything else in war, is being spent. And one day there may come a morning when the guns finally fall silent – and the terrible discovery will be that there is almost nothing left to hear the silence.

articles.title: Ukraine is agonizing – Kremlin
articles.body:
Ukraine in ‘final manifestations of agony’ – Kremlin
Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure, including the raid on St. Petersburg, are no more than desperate attempts by Kiev to change the course of the conflict and will not succeed, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
One person was killed and five others wounded in St. Petersburg during an overnight aerial raid by the Ukrainian military, according to local governor Aleksandr Beglov. The attack also damaged over a dozen apartment blocks and caused a fire at a local oil terminal.
Peskov described the attack as “some final manifestations of agony” of Ukraine, adding that, although “the Kiev regime is fighting back, it cannot alter the course of history.”
According to the Kremlin spokesman, Russia has been consistently responding to the Ukrainian attacks with major systematic strikes, which “do yield results.”
Moscow has accused Kiev of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure and residential areas with long-range drones in an attempt to compensate for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
Kiev also continues to target Russian oil infrastructure despite demands by US President Donald Trump to curb the attacks, which he blames for surging global energy prices. Trump had previously accused Vladimir Zelensky of “making problems” for the US and the whole world and suggested that Ukraine needs a “new president.”
Washington also struck a deal with Moscow earlier this month to alleviate the fuel crisis ahead of the midterm US election on November 3. The agreement involved the US easing restrictions on Moscow’s diesel exports and waiving the “bone-crushing” sanctions, including 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas in exchange for Moscow supplying diesel to the global market and potentially to the US as well.
Russia has responded to Kiev’s terrorist attacks by intensifying its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and logistics infrastructure. The Russian Defense Ministry maintains that the nation’s forces do not target civilians, and the strikes are targeting only military targets and infrastructure supporting the Ukrainian forces.

articles.title: Rubio heads to Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
articles.body:
Rubio heads to Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
WASHINGTON, Oct 18 - While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio travels on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.
The top US diplomat is scheduled to land in Samarkand on Sunday to meet with leaders from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump's predecessors.
Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel. Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly last September.
Regional politics aside, the trip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign-policy portfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance.
For instance, Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state. He was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April.
Rubio's previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland.
Trump administration officials have typically rejected any suggestion that cabinet-level officials should focus their travels on geopolitical capitals and hot spots.
Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, for instance, said on X last week that the idea only certain destinations were worthy of visits from secretaries of state "perfectly encapsulates the decadence and degeneracy of the contemporary US foreign policy establishment."
US-RUSSIA RELATIONS LOOM
One Central Asian diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said officials in the region are wondering to what extent the US will continue targeting Russian sanctions evasion. All C5 states, while drawing closer to the US, have deep historical ties with Moscow, and the region has facilitated Russian imports and exports that violate US and European Union sanctions, Western officials say.
In the past, the US has pushed regional states to clamp down on those illicit flows.
But Trump struck a deal with Moscow this month to import Russian diesel, a move to lower domestic fuel prices before the congressional midterm elections. On Friday, Trump waived all provisions of legislation that would have allowed him to slap massive tariffs on some nations that buy significant amounts of Russian crude or otherwise help Moscow evade sanctions. Among the nations that could have been affected, experts have said, are India and Kazakhstan.
India, which Rubio will visit after Uzbekistan, remains the world's No. 2 Russian crude importer after China, despite Trump saying in February that India had agreed to stop buying oil from Russia.
Additional questions hang over a potential trade deal with India and an expansion of the Abraham Accords in Central Asia.
A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, described the trade deal on Friday as "pretty much done," raising the possibility that an agreement could be announced during the Rubio trip.
Separately, the US has talked to additional Central Asian nations about joining the Abraham Accords, Reuters reported last year, conversations that could in theory continue in Samarkand.
More than 200 business executives will accompany Rubio to Uzbekistan, the State Department said. The Central Asian diplomat said the Trump administration has focused its commercial efforts on expanding access to the area's rare earth mineral resources.
The trip to Uzbekistan was largely organized by Sergio Gor, the US ambassador to India, the Central Asian diplomat said. Gor, who was born in Uzbekistan and is a friend of Rubio, also serves as the US special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs.
After Uzbekistan, Rubio will visit the Indian cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar to meet with business leaders, including Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani, who earned the Trump administration's favor earlier in the year by backing a new refinery in Texas. Rubio most recently visited India five months ago.
The trip is due to wrap up on Thursday. REUTERS

articles.title: Araghchi’s Baghdad diplomacy: Hormuz, regional security and Muslim unity top Iran’s agenda
articles.body:
Araghchi’s Baghdad diplomacy: Hormuz, regional security and Muslim unity top Iran’s agenda
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has used a series of diplomatic meetings in Baghdad to press for an end to military escalation in West Asia, outline Iran’s conditions for restoring security in the Strait of Hormuz and call for a more active role for the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in addressing disputes among Muslim countries.
Araghchi traveled to the Iraqi capital to attend the 52nd session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers, where he held talks with Iraqi officials and counterparts from Lebanon, Egypt and Algeria, as well as the organization’s secretary-general. His engagements focused on regional security, the Palestinian issue, bilateral relations and diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation.
In remarks on the sidelines of the meeting on Sunday, Araghchi reiterated that Iran remained prepared to defend its national interests while pursuing diplomacy, provided negotiations respected Iran’s rights and were conducted on an appropriate basis.
Strait of Hormuz: Iran sets out seven-point plan for reopening
Araghchi said the insecurity affecting the Strait of Hormuz and its economic consequences for regional countries and the wider international community were a direct result of US-Israeli military aggression against Iran.
He said Tehran had presented Washington with a seven-point plan setting out its conditions for resolving the confrontation. The United States had submitted its own views, which Iran was reviewing, he added.
According to Araghchi, the proposed framework provides a clear path toward restoring security in the strategic waterway if Washington meets Iran’s conditions.
“If our conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen on the sixth day, and negotiations will begin on the seventh day,” he said.
The foreign minister stressed that Iran’s conditions were not extraordinary, arguing that they concerned commitments the United States had previously undertaken under an earlier memorandum of understanding and in other negotiations. He said Washington could implement the requirements within days if it genuinely sought to reopen the strait.
Araghchi also briefed Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein on ongoing diplomatic consultations related to regional peace and security. He reiterated that Iran remained committed to diplomacy as a means of preventing further escalation, even as it maintained its readiness to defend its national security.
The issue also featured in Araghchi’s meeting with Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, during which the two officials discussed bilateral relations, regional and international developments, and diplomatic consultations conducted through mediators.
Araghchi told Abdelatty that Iran had consistently pursued diplomacy with the aim of reducing tensions, while accusing Washington of repeatedly violating its commitments. He cited a US breach of its pledge just two weeks after the signing of a memorandum of understanding intended to end the war.
Iraq ties and the need for regional dialogue
In his meeting with Hussein, Araghchi highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation between Iran and Iraq, particularly in economic, trade and security affairs.
The two ministers also discussed developments in the Arabian Peninsula and ways to help end regional conflicts. Araghchi emphasized that Iran was prepared to facilitate dialogue between parties involved in regional disputes.
Araghchi also met Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi during his visit to Baghdad. No further details of their discussions were immediately available.
Beyond bilateral ties, Araghchi argued that Muslim countries needed to strengthen dialogue and solidarity to address shared challenges, particularly the Palestinian issue and the continued expansionism of the Israeli regime.
OIC urged to play a stronger role in resolving disputes
Araghchi called on the OIC to play a more effective role in resolving differences among Muslim countries and strengthening cooperation across the Islamic world.
He said he had raised the issue in meetings with the Iraqi prime minister, Hussein, and the organization’s newly appointed Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed.
During his meeting with Cheikh Ahmed, the secretary-general expressed the organization’s interest in drawing on Iran’s experience and capabilities to develop initiatives for mediation and dispute settlement among Muslim countries.
Araghchi welcomed the prospect of a more active OIC role, stressing that the organization’s secretariat should operate professionally and impartially and avoid any perception of bias toward or against member states.
He also emphasized the importance of strengthening solidarity among Muslim countries in confronting common challenges, particularly those arising from developments in occupied Palestine.
The foreign minister noted that the OIC had lost some of its influence in recent years and expressed hope that Iraq’s assumption of the rotating presidency, together with the appointment of a new secretary-general, would help revitalize the organization.
Yemen Resolution: Iran insists on fairness, balance and a political solution
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that Iran will not join the consensus on a proposed resolution on Yemen at the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) unless the final text reflects fairness and balance, stressing that Tehran’s position will depend on the wording ultimately adopted.
Speaking to IRNA on Sunday on the sidelines of the annual session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad, Araghchi said the organization’s resolutions had not yet been adopted and that the final communiqué was still being drafted. He noted that Iranian diplomats had engaged in extensive discussions in recent days to ensure that Iran’s views were reflected in the documents, adding that most of the proposed resolutions, with a few exceptions, repeated texts adopted the previous year.
On Yemen, Araghchi said serious discussions had taken place among member states, with Saudi Arabia, Iran and other countries presenting their respective positions. The draft resolution had yet to be finalized, he said, expressing hope that the final text would reflect a fair and balanced approach. If these principles were not upheld, Iran would be unable to join the consensus and would formally register its reservations or reject the resolution, depending on its final wording.
Araghchi acknowledged that countries aligned with Saudi Arabia constituted a sizable bloc within the OIC, but said Tehran had conducted extensive consultations and clearly outlined its position on a just solution to the conflict. He stressed that Yemen’s crisis could not be resolved through military force or blockade, calling instead for a political process grounded in the United Nations Charter, respect for Yemen’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and protection of the Yemeni people’s human rights. He also offered Iran’s assistance in facilitating dialogue among the parties.
Rejecting allegations that Yemen’s armed forces had attacked Mecca and Medina, Araghchi said repeating such accusations would neither serve the interests of the Muslim world nor strengthen unity among OIC member states. He emphasized that the sanctity of Islamic holy sites must be respected by all.
Lebanon: Iran stresses sovereignty while acknowledging political differences
Araghchi’s meeting with Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji focused on bilateral relations, Lebanon’s sovereignty and national security, and regional developments.
Araghchi reaffirmed Iran’s support for Lebanon’s territorial integrity and its efforts to defend its sovereignty and national security against Israeli military action and expansionism.
Speaking separately to reporters, he described his meeting with Rajji as respectful but serious and frank, acknowledging differences between Tehran and the current Lebanese government over approaches to regional and domestic issues.
Nevertheless, he stressed that both countries had an interest in maintaining and developing relations.
“I emphasized that the Islamic Republic of Iran is interested in having comprehensive political, economic and cultural relations with Lebanon as a country,” Araghchi said.
He added that Lebanon’s internal affairs were for the Lebanese people to decide. Referring to Hezbollah, he described the movement as one of Lebanon’s most important political groups and an established part of the country’s political and social landscape.
Araghchi said decisions made by Lebanese political groups, including Hezbollah, should be treated as matters of Lebanon’s domestic affairs.
Algeria: Palestinian issue remains central to Muslim solidarity
In a meeting with Sofiane Chaib, Algeria’s secretary of state to the minister of foreign affairs, Araghchi discussed bilateral relations and developments affecting the Muslim world, with particular emphasis on Palestine.
He described Palestine as the foremost concern facing the Muslim world and humanity, citing the continued Israeli occupation and the situation in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Araghchi called for stronger unity and solidarity among Muslim countries to end Israel’s impunity and to confront its continued expansionism.
He also briefed the Algerian official on developments in West Asia and US interventionist and destabilizing actions in the Persian Gulf region.
Alongside his meetings in Baghdad, Araghchi held a telephone conversation on Sunday with Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar.
According to Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry, the two officials discussed bilateral relations and regional developments and stressed the importance of dialogue and diplomacy amid continuing regional tensions.
The conversation added to the diplomatic contacts surrounding efforts to prevent further escalation and address outstanding regional disputes.
Diplomacy and defense remain parallel priorities
Across his meetings and public remarks in Baghdad, Araghchi presented diplomacy as a central instrument for addressing regional crises, while maintaining that Iran would defend its national interests and security.
His message combined calls for stronger cooperation among neighboring countries, a more active OIC role in resolving disputes, and greater unity among Muslim states over Palestine with a clear warning that progress on the Strait of Hormuz depended on Washington meeting Tehran’s stated conditions.
The meetings also highlighted the range of issues confronting regional diplomacy, from maritime security and the economic repercussions of conflict to Yemen, Lebanon and the future of Palestinian territories.
For Tehran, Araghchi’s Baghdad engagements provided an opportunity to advance bilateral ties, engage regional counterparts and press for diplomatic solutions while reiterating Iran’s position that lasting security requires respect for national sovereignty and the fulfillment of commitments.

articles.title: Ukraine prepares two low-cost domestic missiles for combat use against jet-powered Geran drones
articles.body:
Ukraine prepares two low-cost domestic missiles for combat use against jet-powered Geran drones
Two Ukrainian teams are preparing domestically developed surface-to-air missiles for combat use against Russian jet-powered drones.
Source: Andrii Hrytseniuk, head of the Ukrainian defence-tech cluster Brave1, in an interview with Ukrainska Pravda
Details: "They are cheap and easy to manufacture. One of the requirements was to keep the cost of a missile below US$20,000," Hrytseniuk said.
The ambition of these projects is underscored by the average market cost of missiles, ranging from hundreds of thousands of dollars per shot for a Stinger to half a million dollars for an AIM-9X missile used by F-16 fighter jets.
Even using two or three such missiles against a Russian long-range drone is expected to be cost-effective relative to the value of the target. Various estimates put the cost of a standard Geran at around US$70,000, while its jet-powered version may cost tens of thousands of dollars more.
Hrytseniuk said Brave1 began funding the development of surface-to-air missiles in 2024. It took two years to produce the first prototypes. A total of 10 Ukrainian teams are working on such missiles.
Background: In May, it was reported that Ukraine is developing low-cost interceptor missiles and had already tested some solutions. Then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said there were plans to scale up their production dozens of times.

articles.title: Ukraine FM says Russian-held town is a 'death trap' with starving residents, Zelensky says genocide
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Saturday that Russian occupying forces were turning the Ukrainian town of Oleshky into a "death trap" gripped by starvation, and urged international organizations to help evacuate its residents.
Sybiha made his comments on X/Twitter a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged, in a conversation with Pope Leo, to cooperate in delivering vital supplies into the town in southern Ukraine's Kherson region.
"Russians are trying to turn the Ukrainian town of Oleshky into a death trap. The hospital has run out of medicine. Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in homes, as Russians forbid residents from burying them," Sybiha wrote.
"Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, preserves and even snails... Ukraine has repeatedly called for safe evacuation and international humanitarian access. These appeals cannot remain unanswered."
The Kremlin acknowledged in September that Oleshky had critical problems with food and medical supplies but said Russia's military was working to resolve them. Ukraine's military has twice used drones to deliver food and medicine to the town.
UN, Red Cross urged to secure evacuations, humanitarian access
Sybiha urged the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and other organizations to "secure safe evacuation corridors and immediate humanitarian access."
Oleshky lies on the east side of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region, which Russian forces mostly occupied soon after the 2022 invasion. A Ukrainian counteroffensive later recaptured large chunks of territory, including the city of Kherson.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy described the situation in Oleshky this week as "genocide."
Oleshky had a pre-war population of 24,000 people and is now home to around 1,700 residents, including 47 children, according to Danielle Bell, head of the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
Local prosecutors said on Saturday Russian forces dropped aerial bombs on the city of Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro from Oleshky, killing an ambulance driver and wounding 40 people.

articles.title: Vance acknowledges ‘failures’ in US handling of Iran war
articles.body:
US Vice President JD Vance acknowledged “a lot of mistakes and a lot of fundamental failures” in the handling of the Iran war, as he faced questions over the conflict’s rising human and economic costs during a CBS News town hall, Anadolu reports.
Vance made the remarks in response to Joey Amor, whose wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, was among six US Army Reserve soldiers killed in an Iranian strike on a military site in Kuwait in the opening hours of the war that began in late February. At least 21 US service members have been killed and hundreds wounded so far.
Amor questioned reports that the facility had not been adequately secured, demanding accountability from the Trump administration.
“Though the Iranian drone was the weapon that killed my wife, there were a lot of mistakes and a lot of fundamental failures that led up to that,” Amor said.
Vance acknowledged that there were shortcomings. “Sometimes information doesn’t filter up to me,” he said, pledging to “take every single failure extremely seriously.”
The vice president also admitted that the positioning of US troops exposed weaknesses in the military’s approach. “I know that there are some issues with, for example … where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake and that we could do better on. And we have changed that,” he said.
Vance pointed to the growing threat posed by inexpensive drones, saying the US military had altered its tactics to better protect troops and prevent further casualties.
Asked why Washington had still not secured a decisive victory despite President Donald Trump’s initial expectations, Vance argued that the US had “in some ways … won decisively,” but acknowledged the outcome also depended on Iran’s actions. “The enemy gets a vote here,” he said.
Vance defended the administration’s strategy, saying Washington was seeking a “final firm commitment from the Iranians that they’re not going to rebuild their nuclear program.”

articles.title: Drones Hit St. Petersburg Oil Terminals, VK Data Center, and Bridge
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone attack early Sunday morning, Oct. 18, struck fuel transshipment infrastructure, a major enterprise data center, a logistics warehouse, and a highway bridge across St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region, sparking multiple fires and knocking out power to 20,000 residents.
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the municipality came under attack by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overnight, resulting in blazes across four city districts.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Beglov acknowledged impacts at the Petersburg Oil Terminal (PNT) alongside damage to additional infrastructure sites, while claiming that emergency responders had been dispatched to contain localized fires.
According to independent Russian outlet Astra, municipal emergency warning systems failed to notify residents ahead of the strikes, with alerts transmitted either after impacts had occurred or with substantial operational delays.
Open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis conducted by Astra verified that fires erupted at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Baltic region’s primary petroleum transshipment hub.
Concurrently in the city’s Krasnogvardeisky district, drone debris ignited a blaze at the “Ruchyi” oil depot. The Ruchyi fuel depot maintains an operational capacity of 3,900 cubic meters, functioning as a bulk storage and loading facility for AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline alongside commercial diesel.
Mushrooms and the Autumn Moon
Hits on VK data center, substation, and Ozon logistics depot
The overnight assault extended across the administrative boundary into the Leningrad region, targeting corporate digital backbones and electrical distribution facilities.
In the village of Novosergievka in the Vsevolozhsk district, strike drones hit a large server data center owned by Russian technology giant VK (VKontakte).
Although VK company representatives claimed corporate services continued operating normally, users across Russia reported widespread connection dropouts and outages affecting the VKontakte social media platform and its integrated ecosystem.
Astra’s OSINT analysts established that an electrical substation located adjacent to the VK data center was also damaged during the strike.
Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed that damage to electrical distribution installations triggered emergency power cuts, leaving approximately 20,000 residents in the area without electricity.
Separately, Russian e-commerce company Ozon confirmed that an aerial impact sparked a fire at its fulfillment center in St. Petersburg’s Kolpino district on Sofiyskaya Street.
Operating as one of Ozon’s busiest logistics facilities in northwestern Russia, the hub spans up to 79,000 square meters.
The company reported that emergency brigades contained the blaze and confirmed no personnel were injured.
Strike on Western High-Speed Diameter bridge
Drone impacts were also recorded on municipal transport arteries. According to Astra, a drone struck the cable-stayed bridge spanning the Korabelny fairway in St. Petersburg, located roughly 4.5 kilometers from the Petersburg Oil Terminal.
The bridge forms a critical section of the southern viaduct of the Western High-Speed Diameter (WHSD), a multi-lane toll expressway connecting northern and southern sectors of the metropolis.
Municipal engineering teams were deployed to evaluate structural damage to the suspension cables and road deck.
The multi-site strikes in St. Petersburg and Leningrad region reflect an expanding Ukrainian asymmetric campaign to degrade Russian rear logistics, petroleum transshipment, and corporate digital logistics.
The incident follows consecutive strikes on Russian technology hubs earlier in the month, including attacks that disabled Yandex data centers in Vladimir, Ryazan, and Kaluga regions, alongside reported strikes on a Sberbank data center facility in Saratov region.
